claims.claim: AI will need so much energy we have to burn more fossil fuels to keep up
heard_as: AI will make emissions explode
We can't decarbonise while running AI
ChatGPT is destroying the climate
AI is a fossil fuel technology
We need to burn more gas to power AI
Nuclear is the only way to run AI
Data centres will consume half the grid
claims.kernel: Because the raw numbers being thrown around sound enormous, and because tech companies themselves are behaving as if the concern is real — striking gas deals, restarting nuclear plants, buying up interconnects. Every week brings a headline about a hyperscale project needing a whole nuclear reactor. If your reference point is Meta buying 10 gas plants to power a single Louisiana data centre, "AI is a fossil fuel problem" looks like a factual observation.
claims.truth: The picture is much smaller and more manageable than the headlines suggest: - **Data centres use around 1 to 3% of world electricity today**, even including AI - The often-quoted "AI search uses 10× the energy of a Google search" line came from **Alphabet's chairman in 2023**; tech companies have not published real numbers to verify it since - **IEA forecast: world electricity demand grows by ~6,000 TWh by 2030**. Data centres account for only **~3% of that growth** - Larger drivers of the 2023-2030 electricity increase are, in order: **industry, buildings, electric vehicles, air conditioning and heating** - Even under pessimistic scenarios where AI demand doubles or triples, data centres reach **~6% of global electricity**, not a "civilisation-ending" number - **Location matters more than the global total.** In Ireland, data centres are 17% of national electricity; in more than five US states, at least 10%. That is a real siting and grid problem, not a global-emissions problem - Personal AI use is trivial: 100 ChatGPT questions ≈ **streaming a 20-minute video** or **running an electric heater for one minute** - **History rhymes**: in the late 1990s people predicted data centres would eat over half of US electricity. Between 2010 and 2018, global compute grew 550% while data centre energy use only grew 6% — thanks to steady efficiency gains ("Koomey's Law")
claims.say_this: AI will use more electricity. The problem is real, but not the size the headlines make it. Data centres are around 1 to 3% of world electricity today, and even under pessimistic AI scenarios that maybe doubles by 2030. The IEA expects industry, buildings, EVs, air conditioning and heating to each add more to global demand than data centres do. The real issue is that tech companies are dashing for gas because they want power right now — not because clean power cannot cover it if we plan properly.

pushback.if: But look at all the new gas plants being built for data centres.
pushback.reply: That is the real problem. It is not that AI needs fossil fuels, it is that tech companies want power **immediately** and gas is the fastest thing to plug into an existing grid. Which is a policy choice, not a physical necessity. Solar + storage, hydro, geothermal and existing nuclear can all serve the same demand if given the same lead time.

pushback.if: AI could triple electricity demand.
pushback.reply: Even in the most pessimistic public forecasts, that pushes data centres to ~6% of global electricity, not a runaway. And "could" is doing a lot of work in that sentence — efficiency has consistently beaten the panic scenarios for 40 years of computing history.

pushback.if: Individuals should stop using AI to reduce their footprint.
pushback.reply: Not really where the leverage is. Personal AI use is somewhere between negligible and rounding error compared to driving, flying, heating a home, or diet. The pressure that changes anything is on **tech companies to source clean power and publish real numbers**, not on individuals to skip a chatbot query.

claims.claim: air conditioning is a luxury the climate can't afford
heard_as: AC is destroying the climate
We can't afford air conditioning for everyone
AC use should be rationed
It's a lifestyle issue
The West should give up AC first
People survived without AC before
AC drives the climate crisis
claims.kernel: Because AC does use a lot of electricity, and it does contribute to grid strain on the hottest days. The direct emissions are real. And it's easy to frame it as a "rich person's problem" when the countries with the most AC per capita are wealthy ones like the US. If you look at the electricity draw of the US on a July afternoon and worry that India getting to the same level would break the planet, "AC is a luxury we can't afford" sounds sensible.
claims.truth: - Around **2 billion AC units** in the world today; expected to reach **6 billion by 2050** — a tripling - AC is already **3-4% of world greenhouse gas emissions** and uses about **8% of world electricity** - Growth is driven by rising incomes in low- and middle-income countries — people who cannot currently afford cooling finally can - **Heating still causes about 4× more global emissions than cooling** — the "cooling is the climate crisis" framing has the emissions ratio backwards **Efficient units cut demand nearly in half:** - Business as usual (today's typical inefficient units): global cooling electricity demand reaches **6,200 TWh by 2050**, up from 2,000 TWh in 2020 - Switch to efficient units that already exist: demand only reaches **3,400 TWh** - The difference is about the size of the **entire EU's electricity use** **Why inefficient units dominate:** - Cost. Poor households buying their first AC often can't afford the extra $100 for the efficient model. That price gap dooms them to years of higher electricity bills — a family buying a 50% more efficient unit could save around **$2,000** over the following years. **Grid strain (real, but manageable with efficiency):** - **US**: cooling is already ~30% of peak electricity demand on hot days. With efficient units, that could fall to just over 20% by 2050 - **India**: cooling is ~10% of peak today; with inefficient units, that could rise to ~45% by 2050 — a massive grid strain. With efficient units, only ~20%. **Solar helps.** Cooling peaks when the sun shines. Solar generation aligns almost perfectly with AC demand, so a grid with lots of solar can meet cooling demand without a huge rise in emissions.
claims.say_this: Cooling saves lives, helps kids learn, lets people sleep and work. As the world warms, it's a necessity, not a luxury. The number of AC units will roughly triple by 2050 — that's mostly people escaping heat, which is a good thing. What we need to worry about is efficiency: switching everyone to efficient units instead of cheap inefficient ones would cut cooling electricity demand nearly in half. Heating still causes four times more emissions than cooling anyway.

pushback.if: AC is causing the climate to warm even more.
pushback.reply: Some, yes — but heating still emits 4× more. If your worry is emissions, look at heating first. If your worry is grid strain, the fix is efficient units, not banning AC.

pushback.if: But people in Asia getting AC will double emissions.
pushback.reply: Only if they buy inefficient units, and only if the electricity is coal. **Efficient units + solar-heavy grids** cut cooling emissions to a small fraction of the naïve projection. The transition to efficient AC is one of the cheapest emissions wins available.

pushback.if: Rich people don't need it, they should just adapt.
pushback.reply: Rich people already have it. The people who most urgently need it — for basic health and productivity — are lower-income households in tropical countries where heat is now dangerous. Framing cooling as unnecessary luxury effectively means telling those households to sweat it out. That is not a viable climate policy.

claims.claim: we can just keep burning fossil fuels and capture the CO2
heard_as: Carbon capture will fix it
We can just capture the CO2
Why cut fossil fuels when we can just clean up the CO2?
CCS is the answer
Direct air capture will save us
We can suck the carbon out of the sky later
Net zero doesn't mean zero, it means capture the rest
claims.kernel: Because CCS is a real technology and it does work when it works. It sounds like exactly the kind of engineering fix a wealthy society should be able to build: keep the existing power plants and factories, bolt on a capture unit at the top of the chimney, pump the CO2 underground, done. It also comes from serious voices — oil companies, IPCC reports, government net-zero plans — so people assume it must be doing more than it is.
claims.truth: CCS today captures a very small share of global emissions and its track record is poor: - **CCS is running at 45 sites worldwide**, capturing about **50 million tonnes of CO2 per year** — around **0.1% of global emissions** (Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World*) - **Around 50 more plants could be online by 2030**, taking the total to about **0.4% of emissions** - Even in a very optimistic scenario where CCS captures **1 billion tonnes a year by 2030** (a number that appears in many net-zero plans), that is still only **2% of world emissions** - Track record is bad: by 2020, **149 CCS projects were meant to be running; more than 100 were cancelled** - In the US, **around 80% of CCS projects have failed**, mostly due to cost and technology readiness Where CCS could genuinely help is a narrow list: **the last 20-30% of electricity** in regions with poor sun and wind, and hard-to-decarbonise industries like **cement, steel and fertiliser (~15% of world emissions)**. For transport and most electricity, there is no useful role — solar, wind and batteries do the job cheaper. Cost matters too. Oxford researchers modelled two paths: one where CCS handles half of all emission cuts, and one where it handles a tenth. The high-CCS path costs **over $1 trillion more per year**, tens of trillions by 2050.
claims.say_this: Carbon capture and storage is real and it does have a role, but it is not a way out of burning less fossil fuel. Today all the CCS plants in the world capture around one thousandth of global emissions. Even in the most optimistic 2030 case it is about 2%. We still have to cut fossil fuels fast, and use CCS only where nothing cheaper works, like cement and steel.

pushback.if: So we should invest heavily in CCS then?
pushback.reply: Some investment is worthwhile so the technology can improve, but it should get much less funding than solar, wind, batteries and electrification. Using CCS heavily is far more expensive than using it only where nothing else works.

pushback.if: Isn't it in every credible net-zero plan?
pushback.reply: Yes, but it is treated as a **small residual solution** for the hard cases (cement, steel, fertiliser), not a substitute for cutting fossil fuel use. When oil companies present CCS as their central strategy, that is a different claim from what climate scientists are saying.

pushback.if: Fossil fuel companies can afford it — why not just make them pay?
pushback.reply: They can and they should. In 2022 they made **$4 trillion in profit**. At roughly $100 to capture one tonne, that would have paid to capture 40 billion tonnes, more than a year of global emissions. The problem is not the money, it is the political will to make them do it. And even then, capture would not solve the other side effects of fossil fuel extraction — air pollution, methane leaks, spills, land use.

claims.claim: China emits more than us, so why should we bother
heard_as: we're only 1% of global emissions
China opens a coal plant every week
nothing we do matters while they keep building
claims.kernel: China is the largest annual emitter, at roughly 30% of global CO2, and it is still building coal plants. Those facts are correct and pretending otherwise costs you credibility instantly.
claims.truth: Three things are missing. Per person, Chinese emissions are well below American ones. Historically, the US and Europe put up the majority of the CO2 already in the atmosphere, and it stays there for centuries, so the warming we have now is largely ours. And on action, China installs more solar and wind than the rest of the world combined and dominates manufacturing of the panels, batteries and EVs everyone else is buying. The premise that they are doing nothing has not been true for years.
claims.say_this: China emits the most in total and about half as much per person as the US. It also installs more solar and wind than the rest of the world put together, so they are not the ones standing still.

pushback.if: They're still building coal plants
pushback.reply: They are, and it is a real problem. They are also building more clean power than everyone else combined. Both are true at once.

pushback.if: But we're tiny, it makes no difference
pushback.reply: Every country under 2% adds up to about a third of global emissions. If small means exempt, a third of the problem is exempt.

sources.label: Our World in Data, CO2 emissions

claims.claim: clean energy relies on child labour and exploitation
heard_as: EVs run on child labour
Green energy = blood diamonds
You're powering your Tesla with cobalt from Congo mines
Renewables aren't ethical
Clean tech has a dirty secret
Electric cars exploit African workers
claims.kernel: Because the reporting on cobalt mining in the DRC is horrifying and accurate. Children do work in artisanal mines. People do die in mine collapses. Toxic exposure damages workers' health. Anyone who reads about it is right to be angry — and right to worry about whether an EV in their driveway is complicit. The mistake is applying that concern only to clean tech while ignoring the same cobalt in the phone in your pocket and the historical cobalt used in petrol car catalytic converters.
claims.truth: **Cobalt — the "blood diamond of batteries":** - **74% of world cobalt is mined in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)** - Informal DRC mining is often brutally exploitative — hundreds of thousands of workers, including children, paid a few dollars a day - Mine collapses, falling rocks, chemical exposure and eye damage are common - **EVs are now the biggest single use of cobalt: 45%.** **Electronics (phones, laptops) use 26%.** **Context on the DRC itself:** - **>60%** of people live on less than **$2 a day** - **80%** don't have electricity or safe drinking water - **Mining is 90%** of the country's exports and a vital income source for millions **Other minerals with governance risks:** - **~50% of world mineral reserves** are in countries with "weak" or "poor" governance scores - **94% of rare earths, 70% of cobalt, 59% of nickel, 41% of copper, 34% of lithium** are in these countries **Signs of change:** - **BloombergNEF cobalt forecasts keep falling.** In 2019 it predicted over **300,000 tonnes** of cobalt needed by 2030. Three years later, that forecast was **under 150,000 tonnes**. - **Tesla now puts LFP (no cobalt) batteries in more than half its new cars** - **BYD** is investing in **sodium-ion batteries** — no cobalt, no lithium - **EU Critical Raw Materials Act (2023)** forces regular supply chain audits and caps how much of a mineral can come from a single country
claims.say_this: Exploitation in mineral supply chains is real — cobalt from the Democratic Republic of Congo especially, where children work in unsafe informal mines. It's an urgent problem. But it isn't unique to clean energy. Your phone, your laptop and even parts of the fossil fuel supply chain use the same cobalt from the same mines. And clean energy is one of the few industries actually moving away from cobalt — Tesla, BYD, Chinese battery makers. This is a problem to fix, not a reason to keep burning coal.

pushback.if: So EVs are built on child labour.
pushback.reply: Some of them, partly, yes. So is the phone in your pocket. So is fossil fuel refining (cobalt is used as a catalyst in petrol engines). This isn't an EV problem — it's a global supply chain problem, and clean energy is one of the sectors moving away from cobalt fastest.

pushback.if: We should boycott these countries.
pushback.reply: Simple, wrong answer. Mining is a huge share of DRC income and one of the main livelihoods there. Cutting the country out entirely would push millions further into poverty without fixing the exploitation. The right answer is **reforming supply chains** — better wages, safer conditions, getting children into school. That's harder than boycotting, but actually helps people.

pushback.if: Switching to LFP batteries fixes everything.
pushback.reply: It removes cobalt from that specific battery — a real win. But LFP still uses lithium, which comes with its own mining and water concerns. Sodium-ion batteries use neither cobalt nor lithium. Each generation of the technology has fewer contested inputs. The trajectory is genuinely improving.

pushback.if: Rich countries just import the problem.
pushback.reply: Also true. The rich countries buying phones and EVs know what's happening in DRC and don't do enough to change it. Both mining countries and importing countries share responsibility. Improving conditions requires pressure from both ends of the chain.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: clean energy uses too much water to be sustainable
heard_as: EVs use tons of water to make
Lithium mining is draining Chile
Solar panels use lots of water
Green energy is destroying water supplies
Renewables aren't sustainable because of water
It's a water disaster
claims.kernel: Because the local water impacts are real and severe. In parts of northern Chile, mining uses more than half of all the fresh water in the region. Indigenous communities have been badly affected. Investigative journalism on lithium and copper mining focuses on exactly these places. If you're reading that reporting, "mining is killing water supplies" isn't a myth — it's a documented fact in specific places. The mistake is generalising it into "clean energy uses too much water" globally, when the fossil fuel system uses far more.
claims.truth: **Where the local problem is real:** - **16% of critical mineral mines** are in areas with **high water stress** - For **copper and lithium**, about **half of world supply** comes from high or extreme water stress regions - In parts of northern **Chile**, **mining uses over half** of all fresh water — creating serious conflict with local communities **But mining is a small share of overall water use:** - Even in Chile, **mining uses just 4% of water**; **farming uses 72%** **EV vs petrol — today's picture:** - **China**: an EV uses **262 m³** of water over its life vs **137 m³** for petrol — almost double - **US**: an EV uses about **⅓ more water** than a petrol car - Reason: **82%** of the water use comes from **making the electricity**, not building the car or battery — and most electricity today is still fossil fuels **Once electricity goes clean, EVs win on water too:** - EVs charged with **solar or wind** use about **two-thirds less water** than petrol cars **Solar and wind vs fossil energy — the big picture:** - Solar and wind use **5-10× less water than natural gas** per unit of electricity - Solar and wind use **10-100× less water than coal** - Coal, gas and nuclear plants all need huge volumes of water to cool their equipment - Solar panels and wind turbines need essentially none **Water use in the US is already falling** as the country moves from coal → gas → solar and wind.
claims.say_this: Overall, clean energy uses much less water than fossil fuels — coal, gas and nuclear plants all need huge volumes for cooling, and solar and wind don't. The real problem is local: lithium and copper mining happens in a few specific places that are already very short on water, especially northern Chile. EVs also use more water than petrol cars today, but only because they're mostly charged with fossil electricity — with solar and wind, they use two-thirds less.

pushback.if: But EVs use more water than petrol cars.
pushback.reply: Today, yes — because the electricity is mostly fossil fuels. Fossil power plants need enormous amounts of water for cooling, and that shows up in the EV lifecycle. As the grid decarbonises, EVs cross over to using less water than petrol cars. In a solar/wind grid, they use two-thirds less.

pushback.if: Chile is running out of water because of lithium.
pushback.reply: Northern Chile has a real crisis, and lithium brine extraction is part of it. The specific fix is **direct lithium extraction** (DLE) — pulling lithium from brine without evaporating the water. This works and is being deployed. The broader point still stands: lithium mining uses 4% of water in Chile; farming uses 72%. Both need addressing.

pushback.if: So clean energy is fine on water then?
pushback.reply: Locally, no — some mining regions are being pushed to their water limits. Globally, yes — clean energy uses far less water than the fossil system it's replacing. Both things are true.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: Wind turbine blades and solar panels just end up in landfill
heard_as: they're burying blades in the desert
nobody can recycle solar panels
the waste from clean tech will be the next crisis
claims.kernel: There are real photographs of buried blades, and a wave of equipment installed over the last two decades is genuinely reaching end of life now. The problem is not imaginary.
claims.truth: It is a real problem of a modest size. Cumulative solar panel waste could reach 160 million tonnes by 2050. By the same date total e-waste is projected at around 1.8 billion tonnes and plastic waste at over 12 billion tonnes, so solar is a rounding error next to the waste streams nobody campaigns about. Recycling is also scaling fast, especially for batteries. China's GEM recovers over 90% of the lithium from used batteries and processed around 17,000 tonnes of EV batteries in 2022. Redwood Materials found many packs it takes in still hold more than half their capacity, and is repurposing them into solar powered microgrids rather than shredding them.
claims.say_this: Solar waste by 2050 is about 160 million tonnes. Plastic waste will be over 12 billion. It is a real problem, just not the one worth panicking about.

pushback.if: Recycling never actually happens
pushback.reply: For plastic, largely fair. For batteries it is a genuine industry already, because the materials inside are valuable enough to chase.

sources.label: MIT Technology Review, GEM battery recycling
Inside Climate News, solar panel waste reality check

claims.claim: The climate has always changed
heard_as: there were ice ages before humans
it was warmer in medieval times
it's just natural cycles
claims.kernel: Completely true. The climate has changed many times, sometimes dramatically, long before anyone was burning anything.
claims.truth: And every one of those changes had a cause we can name: orbital cycles, volcanic activity, shifts in solar output, changes in ocean circulation. We measure all of those today, and none of them account for the current warming, while the rise tracks CO2 from fossil fuels closely. The other difference is speed. Past natural transitions unfolded over many thousands of years, giving ecosystems time to move. This one is happening over about 150, far faster than anything in the records we have.
claims.say_this: It has, and every time we can name what caused it. The things that caused those changes are all measured today and none of them explain this one.

pushback.if: Scientists said there was a pause in warming
pushback.reply: There was a slower decade, then a surge. Ocean heat kept rising throughout, which is where over 90% of the extra heat goes.

claims.claim: the energy transition will destroy jobs
heard_as: Green jobs won't replace real jobs
The transition will hollow out coal towns
Oil workers will be thrown on the scrap heap
You can't retrain a coal miner as a solar installer
Clean energy pays less than fossil fuels
Climate policy is a war on workers
claims.kernel: Because in specific places and industries it will hurt real people. Coal towns, oil towns, engineering communities built around a refinery — these places do face job losses, and pretending otherwise is dishonest. Anyone who lives in one of these communities and reads a headline about a coal plant closure has good reason to worry. The mistake is generalising that specific pain into "the whole transition destroys jobs."
claims.truth: **Total energy jobs are rising, not falling:** - **63 million in 2019** → **68 million in 2023** - Could reach **72 million by 2030**, or **82 million** on a stronger climate pathway - **Clean energy jobs overtook fossil fuel jobs in 2021** because far more money is now flowing into clean energy **It's happening in rich countries too:** - **US** energy jobs grew **3.8% in 2022** — faster than the economy as a whole. Clean energy jobs specifically grew **3.9%**. - **UK** "green jobs" growing at **4× the normal market rate** **Most clean energy jobs can't be exported:** - Installing solar panels, fitting heat pumps, building EV charging points, insulating homes — these have to happen locally, on the ground. Which makes them politically resilient. **The specific job losses (Ritchie's numbers):** - **~6 million workers** could lose jobs in the traditional car industry (petrol/diesel) by 2030. Roughly **two thirds could move** to related EV or component roles with retraining. VW has pledged to train 22,000, Mercedes has invested >€1.3bn, Ford US has put in >$11bn. - **~2.5 million** could lose oil and gas jobs. About **three quarters could move** into other parts of the energy industry, with proper retraining investment. - **32 million people** globally work in fossil fuels — about **0.4% of world population**. Meanwhile, climate change affects the other 99.6%.
claims.say_this: Jobs in fossil fuels are shrinking, but clean energy jobs are already growing faster. The total number of energy jobs went up from 63 million in 2019 to 68 million in 2023, and clean energy overtook fossil fuels for the first time in 2021. The real problem isn't the total — it's making sure the workers whose jobs shrink get retraining and support, and paid honestly about wage gaps.

pushback.if: But real people in real towns are going to lose their livelihoods.
pushback.reply: Yes. And that is exactly why a **just transition** is not optional. The UK's last coal power station, **Ratcliffe-on-Soar (closed 2023)**, is a working example: most of several hundred workers were moved into other jobs at the company or retrained for partners, with only a handful of forced job losses. It worked because the plan started years before closure — not months.

pushback.if: Wind turbine installers don't earn what oil workers earn.
pushback.reply: True, and it needs to be said honestly. A wind installer typically earns less than an offshore oil worker. Some fossil fuel workers will end up in cleaner jobs at lower pay. Pretending otherwise makes governments look dishonest and workers rightly angry. The fix is direct: **pay clean-energy jobs properly**, and top up transition wages where necessary.

pushback.if: Governments will leave workers stranded when the plant closes.
pushback.reply: They will if they wait until closure is a few months away. The Ratcliffe example shows what works: start planning years ahead, involve the workforce, fund retraining explicitly. This is now a solved policy problem where the political will exists.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: The battery dies after a few years and costs a fortune to replace
heard_as: battery lifetime is horribly uncertain
you'll need a new battery at 8 years
the replacement costs more than the car is worth
claims.kernel: Everyone has had a phone whose battery died within two years, so it is a completely reasonable thing to assume. EV packs are managed and cooled quite differently.
claims.truth: An analysis of 15,000 EVs by Recurrent Motors found only 1.5% had needed a battery replacement, and 90% of cars past 100,000 miles still held at least 90% of their original range. Most manufacturers warrant the pack for eight years as a minimum. Nissan UK reported that almost all of the batteries it has ever made are still in cars, after twelve years of selling them.
claims.say_this: Out of 15,000 EVs studied, 1.5% had needed a new battery. Most cars past 100,000 miles still had 90% of their range.

pushback.if: And then it goes to landfill
pushback.reply: It does not. Packs with half their capacity left are being repurposed into grid storage, and recyclers recover over 90% of the lithium.

claims.claim: An EV has to drive 50,000 miles before it beats a petrol car
heard_as: the battery emissions cancel out the savings
you'd have to drive it for decades to break even
the e-Golf takes 77,000 miles to pay off
the Volvo C40 needs 68,400 miles
claims.kernel: Building a battery really does create more emissions upfront, so an EV starts its life with a carbon debt. That part is true, and it is where the number comes from.
claims.truth: The debt is paid back far faster than the headline figures suggest. Carbon Brief puts the break even point at roughly 11,000 to 13,000 miles in Europe and the UK, under two years of average driving. The very high numbers came from manufacturer studies that overestimated battery emissions, underestimated the emissions from producing petrol, and used lab fuel economy rather than real world figures. Corrected by independent researchers, the VW e-Golf breaks even at about 14,000 miles rather than 77,000, and the Volvo C40 at about 16,000 rather than 68,400.
claims.say_this: The battery does start with a carbon debt. It pays it off in about a year and a half of normal driving, and everything after that is a gain.

pushback.if: But I read it was 70,000 miles
pushback.reply: Those figures came from the carmakers' own studies. Independent researchers rechecked the same cars and got about 15,000 miles.

pushback.if: That is only because you assume clean electricity
pushback.reply: No, those are European grid averages as they are today, and the grid keeps getting cleaner while a petrol car never does.

claims.claim: EVs just move the pollution to the power station
heard_as: the electricity has to come from somewhere
they run on coal
long tailpipe
claims.kernel: The electricity does have to come from somewhere, and on a coal heavy grid an EV genuinely is dirtier than it would be on a clean one. The question is whether it is still better than burning petrol, and it is.
claims.truth: An electric motor is roughly four times more efficient than a combustion engine, so an EV wins even where the grid is dirty. Lifecycle emissions fall by about two fifths in coal heavy Poland and two thirds in the UK. In China, where coal supplied 61% of power in 2022, an EV still breaks even after about 22,000 miles. The 2021 ICCT global study found cuts of 60 to 70% in the US and Europe, 35 to 45% in China and 20 to 35% in India. And an EV keeps improving as the grid decarbonises, while a petrol car is as clean on day one as it will ever be.
claims.say_this: Even on Poland's coal heavy grid an EV cuts emissions by about 40%, because the motor is four times more efficient. And it gets cleaner every year. A petrol car never does.

pushback.if: Not where I live, our grid is fossil heavy
pushback.reply: Fair, the saving is smaller there. It is still a saving, and it grows every year without you doing anything.

claims.claim: Electric cars catch fire and explode
heard_as: they burn down car parks
that ship fire was caused by an EV
you can't put the fire out
claims.kernel: Battery fires behave differently and are harder for firefighters to extinguish, so the concern is not invented. They are also very newsworthy, which is exactly why they feel common.
claims.truth: Norwegian data for 2018 to 2022 records about 30 fires per 100,000 conventional cars a year against about 5 per 100,000 EVs, so petrol and diesel cars catch fire five to six times more often. The Swedish Civil Contingencies Agency puts the gap at twenty times. The EU funded LASH FIRE programme concluded EVs are not more hazardous than conventional cars. The Fremantle Highway cargo ship fire in July 2023 was widely blamed on an EV, and the investigation found the cause was unrelated. The International Union of Marine Insurers stated in August 2023 that no fire on a car carrier had ever been proven to be caused by a factory new EV.
claims.say_this: EV fires make the news precisely because they are rare. Petrol and diesel cars catch fire five to six times more often per vehicle.

pushback.if: But when they do burn you can't stop it
pushback.reply: True, they are harder to put out. That is a firefighting equipment question, not a reason to think they burn more often.

claims.claim: Hydrogen or synthetic fuel is the real answer, not batteries
heard_as: hydrogen cars are more sustainable
e-fuels will save the combustion engine
we should wait for the better technology
claims.kernel: Both technologies are real and both matter, just not for cars. Hydrogen has a serious role in steel, shipping and long haul freight, and e-fuels will likely be needed for aviation.
claims.truth: For passenger cars the energy maths is unforgiving. UK government lifecycle analysis finds hydrogen cars use about three times more energy than EVs with 60 to 70% higher emissions, even assuming low carbon hydrogen. The market has already answered: at the end of 2022 there were 72,000 hydrogen vehicles worldwide against 26 million EVs, a ratio of about 360 to 1. E-fuels cost up to three times more than conventional fuel, need roughly five times more electricity than running an EV, and have lifecycle emissions 53% higher. The IPCC expects the limited supply to go to aviation and shipping.
claims.say_this: Hydrogen and e-fuels matter for planes, ships and steel. For cars they need three to five times more electricity to go the same distance, which is why there are 26 million EVs and 72,000 hydrogen cars.

pushback.if: The technology will improve
pushback.reply: Some, but the losses are thermodynamic, not engineering. You cannot make converting electricity to fuel and back beat using the electricity directly.

claims.claim: The grid can't cope and there aren't enough chargers anyway
heard_as: we'd need 20 new nuclear power stations
the charging network is at crisis point
the lights will go out if everyone plugs in
claims.kernel: Anyone who has queued at a motorway charger knows public charging can be genuinely poor, so the frustration is real even where the numbers are not.
claims.truth: National Grid itself lists the grid claim as a myth. The 2017 headline that Britain would need twenty new nuclear plants was a significant miscalculation and was corrected. Most charging happens at home overnight, off peak, when there is spare capacity on the network. On chargers, UK public charge points passed 50,000 in October 2023, growing 43% year on year against a government target of 300,000 by 2030, and the IEA found charging infrastructure kept pace with EV growth in 2022 with a 55% increase. UK EV sales grew 36% year on year over the first nine months of 2023, which is not what a crisis looks like.
claims.say_this: Most charging happens at home overnight when the grid has spare capacity. National Grid lists this one as a myth on their own website.

pushback.if: I don't have a driveway
pushback.reply: That is the real problem in this argument, and it is worth pressing your council on. It is a rollout gap, not a physics limit.

claims.claim: Keeping my old car running is greener than buying a new EV
heard_as: old bangers are the green choice
the greenest car is the one you already own
manufacturing a new car is worse than running an old one
claims.kernel: It sounds right because you avoid the emissions of building a whole new car, and use what you already have is usually sound environmental advice.
claims.truth: It holds for most products, but not for cars, because a car keeps emitting every day you drive it. A 14 year old petrol car produces around 45 tonnes of CO2 over its remaining life against 14 tonnes for a new Tesla Model Y, a cut of about 68%. Even accounting for the emissions of building the new car, replacing an old petrol car with an EV breaks even after roughly 20,000 to 32,000 miles, about four years of average UK driving.
claims.say_this: For a fridge or a phone, keeping the old one wins. For a car it does not, because most of the damage is in the fuel, not the factory.

pushback.if: So I should scrap a perfectly good car?
pushback.reply: Not scrap. It gets resold and used. The question is what you buy when the old one is genuinely done, and then the EV wins clearly.

claims.claim: Electric cars alone won't solve climate change
heard_as: swapping every car for an electric one isn't the answer
it's just consumerism with a green badge
we need to drive less, not drive electric
claims.kernel: This is true as stated, and it is a fair warning against imagining we can swap every car one for one and carry on exactly as before. Someone saying this is often closer to you than they sound.
claims.truth: It becomes a problem only when it is used as a reason to do nothing. The IPCC judges EVs likely crucial for decarbonising transport, and finds technology adoption could deliver about 50% of land transport emissions reductions by 2050, with a range of 30 to 70%. Infrastructure change contributes around 30% and behaviour change around 5%. So EVs are roughly half the answer, and fewer cars, smaller cars and better public transport are the rest. Both, not either.
claims.say_this: Completely agree, they are about half the answer for transport. The other half is fewer and smaller cars and better public transport. It was never one or the other.

pushback.if: So why push EVs at all?
pushback.reply: Because half is a lot, and because most people are not giving up their car this decade. We can do the easy half while we fight for the hard half.

claims.claim: EVs will soon cost more to run than petrol cars
heard_as: electricity prices will catch up
public charging is more expensive than petrol
wait until they tax the electricity
claims.kernel: There is a real case buried here. If you rely entirely on public rapid charging, the cost per mile can approach petrol, and that is where these stories come from.
claims.truth: Carbon Brief's comparison found EV drivers save on fuel in every country analysed, from the UK and Norway to the US, China, India, Argentina and Australia. Home charging on an off peak tariff costs substantially less than public fast charging, and most drivers charge at home overnight. The UK Climate Change Committee concluded EVs will be significantly cheaper than petrol and diesel vehicles to own and operate over their lifetimes, once servicing and fuel are both counted.
claims.say_this: If you charge at home overnight it is not close. Public rapid charging is where the gap narrows, and most people rarely use it.

pushback.if: They will tax it eventually
pushback.reply: Probably, since fuel duty has to come from somewhere. That is a policy design question, and it does not change the energy cost underneath.

claims.claim: Heavy EVs produce more pollution from tyres and brakes than petrol cars
heard_as: tyre particulates are worse than exhaust
your super heavy EV pollutes more
non-exhaust emissions
claims.kernel: Heavier vehicles do wear tyres faster, and tyre and road dust is a genuine air quality problem that gets far less attention than exhaust fumes. This one has a real core.
claims.truth: The comparison is usually stacked, though. A petrol car has tyre wear and brake wear too, and an exhaust pipe on top of it. EVs also use regenerative braking, which does most of the slowing with the motor and cuts brake dust sharply. Where the argument has genuine force is on size rather than drivetrain: a Hummer EV is responsible for about 341 grams of CO2 per mile, more than a petrol Toyota Corolla at 269 grams, per a 2022 Quartz analysis. The honest version of this point is an argument against enormous cars, not against electric ones.
claims.say_this: Tyre dust is a real problem, and a petrol car has tyres and brakes plus an exhaust. If the worry is heavy vehicles, the target is huge cars, not electric ones.

pushback.if: So you admit big EVs are bad
pushback.reply: Yes, a two and a half tonne electric SUV is a bad answer. So is a two and a half tonne petrol one. Smaller cars win either way.

claims.claim: electric cars catch fire all the time
heard_as: EVs spontaneously combust
Lithium batteries are ticking time bombs
You can't park an EV in an underground garage
One EV fire could take down a whole car park
Fire brigades can't put EV fires out
Electric cars are a fire hazard
claims.kernel: Because EV fires make dramatic headlines. A lithium-ion battery fire burns hot, is hard to extinguish, and produces striking video. Any single EV fire tends to generate coverage that a petrol car fire never would. Repeat that a few times and the perception hardens: "EVs are catching fire." When a big fire in the London airport car park in 2024 was reported as an EV fire, that stuck — even after it turned out to have started in a **diesel Range Rover**.
claims.truth: Data from multiple sources says EVs catch fire less often than petrol cars: - **Global data 2010-2020**: about **0.004% of EVs and plug-in hybrids** caught fire vs **0.08% of petrol cars** — **petrol is 19 times higher** - **Norway** (which has more EVs per capita than anywhere): fewer fires per 100,000 EVs than petrol, diesel or other cars, every year from 2018 to 2022. About **4 fires per 100,000 EVs** on the road — extremely rare - **EV FireSafe**, an Australian Department of Defence-backed group, calculates the risk that a given EV catches fire at **0.0012%**
claims.say_this: EVs actually catch fire much less often than petrol cars — about 19 times less often based on global data. What is true is that when they do catch fire, they are harder to put out. The fear is not proportionate to the risk. The fix is better battery safety and better training for fire services, not going back to petrol.

pushback.if: But when they burn, they burn hotter and longer.
pushback.reply: Correct, and this is the genuine safety issue. Lithium-ion batteries can undergo **thermal runaway** if they short-circuit in a crash — the reaction is self-sustaining and hard to stop. Fires burn hotter than petrol fires and take much longer to put out. The fire brigade needs different techniques and training.

pushback.if: So they're more dangerous when they do happen.
pushback.reply: More difficult to fight, yes. More likely to happen — no, much less likely. The two things are different. A rare fire that is hard to put out can still cause less overall harm than a common fire that is easy to put out.

pushback.if: The EV fleet is newer, so the comparison isn't fair.
pushback.reply: Partly true. EVs on the road are younger on average than petrol cars, and older cars catch fire more often through wear and tear. That may explain some of the gap. But even accounting for age, EVs come out with a lower fire rate.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: electric cars don't work in cold weather
heard_as: EVs die in the cold
Batteries don't work in winter
You can't drive an EV in Canada
The range collapses when it's freezing
EVs are only for warm climates
Norwegian winters kill EVs
claims.kernel: Because the range drop is real. If you compare summer and winter numbers for the same car, the winter figure is genuinely lower. Anyone with an EV who has driven it through a proper winter can confirm this. So this myth doesn't come from nowhere — the honest answer is "yes, a bit."
claims.truth: The most detailed study on this comes from the **Norwegian Automobile Federation (NAF)**, which tested **50 different EV models** in Norway. Same route summer and winter, temperatures 0°C to -10°C: - **Average range drop: 19%.** A car with 450 km advertised range managed about **364 km** in winter. - **Tesla Model Y (best performer): 11% loss** (280 → 226 km) - **Skoda Enyaq iV80 (worst performer): 32% loss** (360 → 245 km) - Similar studies elsewhere find **10 to 20% drops**, so the pattern holds up - **Fast charging is also slower**: 37 minutes average in winter vs 33 in summer — about 10% slower. Some cars (BMW iX) saw charging time jump by a third. For most drivers this rarely matters. In the **US, only about 5% of journeys are longer than 50 km**. Even the worst-affected EV with the biggest range drop still comfortably handles a 100 km round trip in the cold. The real-world confirmation: **Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland and Iceland** — five of the coldest countries in the world — have some of the highest EV adoption rates on Earth.
claims.say_this: EVs do lose range in the cold — typically 10 to 20% — and charging is a bit slower. That is real. But for daily driving (well under 100 miles), it barely matters. And the coldest countries in the world, Norway, Sweden, Finland, all have the highest EV adoption rates. Cold weather is a limitation to plan around, not a reason not to switch.

pushback.if: So EVs lose 20% of their range. That's a lot.
pushback.reply: For a 400 km EV, a 20% drop is still 320 km. Very few people drive that far on a normal day. The situations where it actually matters are long winter road trips, and even those are manageable with one extra charge stop.

pushback.if: Nobody wants to be stuck at a charger in the freezing cold.
pushback.reply: Real concern. Fixes exist: many new EVs have **heat pumps** to warm cabin and battery more efficiently, and **battery pre-heating** before you arrive at the charger cuts charging time back closer to summer levels.

pushback.if: What about very extreme cold, like -30°C?
pushback.reply: Range drops further and public infrastructure gets patchy. The Norwegian tests don't cover Arctic extremes. For -30°C driving, a hybrid or petrol backup might genuinely make more sense — but that is a tiny share of global driving.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: electric cars are just as bad for the climate as petrol cars
heard_as: EVs aren't really green because of the battery
Electric cars have a bigger carbon footprint than petrol cars
The mining and manufacturing cancel out any climate benefit
EVs just move the emissions upstream
Coal-powered EVs are pointless
The lifecycle emissions of an EV are just as bad
claims.kernel: Because the manufacturing footprint is real and non-trivial. Building the battery uses a lot of energy, and a lot of that energy today still comes from fossil fuels. If you stop the analysis at the factory gate, an EV really does start worse than a petrol car. The mistake is stopping the analysis there instead of looking at the whole 15-year life on the road.
claims.truth: Full lifetime emissions (manufacturing + running) show EVs well ahead everywhere: - **UK**: an EV emits **66% less carbon** than a petrol car over its life. By 2030, this rises to **76% less**. - **Europe**: up to **70% lower** lifetime emissions - **US**: about **two thirds lower** - **China** (heavily coal-based grid): still **37 to 45% lower** - **India** (also coal-heavy): **nearly a third lower** These numbers already include emissions from making the car and the battery. EVs will keep getting cleaner as grids decarbonise. Manufacturing is improving fast too: **CATL, the world's largest battery producer, cut its own manufacturing emissions by 45% in a single year** by switching factories to more clean electricity.
claims.say_this: Making an electric car does create more carbon upfront than making a petrol one, mostly because of the battery. But you pay that "carbon debt" back quickly once you start driving, and then the EV keeps being much cleaner for the rest of its life. Over the whole lifetime, an EV is 60 to 70% cleaner than a petrol equivalent almost everywhere, and it keeps improving as electricity grids get greener.

pushback.if: But the battery is a huge carbon debt.
pushback.reply: It is, but you pay it back within about the first 15,000-30,000 miles depending on the grid mix. After that, every mile is far cleaner than a petrol equivalent. Over 150,000 miles the debt is a rounding error compared to the tailpipe emissions you avoid.

pushback.if: What about all the mining?
pushback.reply: Mining is a real problem and needs cleaning up. But a petrol car needs mining plus **continuously extracting and refining and burning oil for 15 years**. The comparison is not "clean vs dirty" — it is "one-off battery mining vs one-off battery mining plus a lifetime of fossil combustion."

pushback.if: OK but for someone who barely drives, it's not worth it.
pushback.reply: Fair. If you barely drive, the climate case for replacing a working petrol car is weak because the manufacturing debt takes a long time to pay off. The best answer for low-mileage drivers is usually to keep the existing car running longer, then go electric when it needs replacing.

claims.claim: electric cars are only good for short trips
heard_as: You can't take an EV on a road trip
Range anxiety is a real thing
EVs are city cars, not proper cars
You'd never make it to Scotland in one
EVs are only good for the school run
The battery dies too fast
claims.kernel: Because the myth is a decade behind the technology. Early EVs really were only good for short trips — the first Nissan Leaf, the BMW ActiveE, all managed less than 100 miles per charge. That was the honest state of the art around 2010-2012. People whose reference point is that era, or who haven't looked closely since, are working from an accurate memory of a very different market.
claims.truth: Range has grown massively in a decade: - **2010 average EV range: ~80 miles** on a single charge - **2021 average: ~220 miles** — nearly triple - **US average (bigger cars are popular): ~450 miles** - Plenty of mainstream models now offer **280+ miles** - Top of the market: in 2011 the longest-range EV (BMW ActiveE) managed **94 miles**. By 2022, the record was **520 miles** (Lucid Air Dream R). The record will keep moving. Daily driving reality: - **Average UK driver: 20 miles/day** (even less if two-car household) - **Average US driver: ~40 miles/day** Both fit comfortably within even the cheapest, lowest-range new EVs. Long trips: on a motorway at the speed limit, you'd cover about **280 miles in 4 hours**. Drivers are advised to take a **15-minute break every few hours anyway**. That lines up with when the EV needs a top-up. Battery degradation is often exaggerated: studies across tens of thousands of vehicles find batteries lose about **2% capacity per year**, much slower than most people assume.
claims.say_this: That was true in 2010, when the average EV had 80 miles of range. It isn't now. Most new EVs comfortably do 200+ miles on a charge, plenty do 400+, and the top of the range is over 500. The average UK driver does 20 miles a day, the average American 40. For daily driving, range is a solved problem. The only real issue left is charging reliability on the occasional long trip.

pushback.if: But I do a 500-mile road trip once a year.
pushback.reply: Two options. Either buy a longer-range EV (they exist), or take one 20-minute charging stop mid-way (which you would take as a break anyway). If it's truly a one-off, some drivers rent a petrol car for that specific trip. Over 15 years of ownership, one long trip a year is not enough to justify choosing a worse daily car.

pushback.if: What if I can't find a charger?
pushback.reply: That's a real concern — but it's a **charging infrastructure** problem, not an EV problem. If your petrol car ran out of fuel because there were no petrol stations, you'd blame the fuel network, not the car. The fix is more reliable public chargers on the routes people drive, not a different car.

pushback.if: Batteries degrade over time so range gets worse.
pushback.reply: By about 2% a year, on average. Over 10 years that's 20% off the starting range. A 300-mile EV becomes a 240-mile EV. Still way beyond the daily need for almost everyone.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: electric cars pollute just as much as petrol cars
heard_as: EVs still pollute
Tyre particles are just as bad as tailpipe emissions
Electric cars aren't zero-emission
PM2.5 from EVs is worse because they're heavier
You're just moving the pollution around
There's no such thing as a clean car
claims.kernel: Because "zero emissions" is a claim EV marketing often makes, and it's technically wrong. Cars pollute in four ways: exhaust, brake wear, tyre wear and road dust. EVs only get rid of one of them. Anyone pointing out that tyre and road particles still exist is telling the truth. The mistake is treating "not zero" as "same as petrol."
claims.truth: The four sources of air pollution from any car: 1. **Tailpipe emissions** — nitrogen oxides (NOx) and PM2.5. Both terrible for respiratory health, both eliminated by EVs. 2. **Brake wear** — friction between pads and discs. EVs use **regenerative braking**, so brakes engage far less often. Much reduced, not eliminated. 3. **Tyre wear** — friction with the road. About the same or slightly worse in EVs, because they're heavier. 4. **Road dust** — kicked up by moving vehicles, also affected by weight. Slightly worse in EVs. Overall verdict: EVs cause slightly higher tyre and road dust pollution, but this is heavily outweighed by removing exhaust emissions and cutting brake wear. Per source-by-source comparison, EVs come out cleaner overall. The remaining problem is real, though — **PM2.5 from non-exhaust sources** still causes real health harm, especially in dense urban areas.
claims.say_this: EVs still cause some pollution — from tyre wear, brake wear and road dust — and being heavier, they're slightly worse on those than petrol cars. But they completely eliminate exhaust pollution, which is by far the biggest and worst source. Overall, they are much better for air quality, not the same. The fix for the rest is making cars lighter and smaller.

pushback.if: So EVs still cause air pollution.
pushback.reply: Yes, some. But the pollution they eliminate — NOx and exhaust PM2.5 — is directly linked to millions of deaths per year worldwide. The pollution they slightly worsen (tyre and road dust) is a smaller problem. Trading one for the other is a big win.

pushback.if: They're heavier because of the battery, so tyre wear is worse.
pushback.reply: True. This is one of the strongest arguments for [smaller EVs](../sectors/transport/smaller-evs-better.md) — a smaller EV with a smaller battery is lighter, cheaper, safer for pedestrians and produces less non-exhaust pollution. Both petrol and electric cars have grown heavier over the past decade, with the "SUV effect" pushing weight up across the board. France has already introduced a weight tax; that logic should apply to EVs too, not just to petrol SUVs.

pushback.if: So EVs aren't really clean.
pushback.reply: The right framing is "much cleaner than petrol on the biggest source, slightly worse on the smaller sources." Not "clean" in the absolute sense. That's why walking, cycling and public transport still beat any car.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: electric cars are too expensive for the average driver
heard_as: Only rich people can afford electric cars
EVs are a luxury
You need to be rich to go green
The savings only work if you own a house with a driveway
Second-hand EVs are just as expensive as new petrol
Once you factor in the charger install, they're not cheaper
claims.kernel: Because the number on the showroom windscreen is genuinely higher. If you're comparing two cars in a dealership today, the EV is usually more expensive to buy. Most people don't think in "total cost of ownership" — they think in monthly payments and the upfront cheque. And for households on tight budgets, that upfront gap is real.
claims.truth: **Running costs are already much cheaper:** - **100 miles in an EV: about £6.** In a petrol car: **£12 to £18** — roughly half or less. - Average UK driver could save up to **£1,000 a year**, over **£10,000 across the life of the car**. - A Gulf Oil study across **33 countries** found EVs cheaper to run than petrol in almost every country surveyed. - EVs have **far fewer moving parts** — no oil changes, no exhaust, no catalytic converter, less brake wear — so maintenance is lower too. **Upfront costs are falling:** - By **2025**, price parity had spread to many mainstream models. The electric Citroën C4 matched the petrol version's price. - **Second-hand** EV versions of best-sellers (BMW, Peugeot, Vauxhall, Hyundai, Tesla) are now often **cheaper than the petrol equivalents**. - **BYD** sells the Seagull in Europe for around **£10,000** with ~250 miles of range, forcing VW, Renault and Stellantis to launch sub-€25,000 EVs. **But charging cost depends on where you charge:** - **Home charging: ~£6** per 100 miles - **Public charger: ~£16** per 100 miles - **Rapid charger: ~£18** per 100 miles (similar to petrol)
claims.say_this: The sticker price of a new EV is still higher than a petrol equivalent, but the gap is closing fast, and running costs are already much lower. Charging at home costs about half what petrol costs, saving the average UK driver around £1,000 a year and over £10,000 across the life of the car. The remaining problem is not "EVs are expensive," it is "cheap EV charging isn't available to everyone."

pushback.if: For someone in a flat with no driveway, EVs aren't cheaper.
pushback.reply: Correct, and this is the real inequality problem inside the EV story. Somebody who can only charge at rapid public chargers pays roughly what a petrol driver pays. Fixing this needs more affordable public and street-side charging, not more EVs.

pushback.if: But I can't afford the upfront £30,000.
pushback.reply: Fair. New EVs are still a stretch. **Used EVs** are now often cheaper than used petrol versions of the same model, and that's where most of the affordable switching will happen in the next few years.

pushback.if: Aren't Chinese EVs being blocked by tariffs?
pushback.reply: Yes, and this is a policy choice that hurts consumers. Some governments have put tariffs on affordable Chinese EVs to protect their own industries. This makes cars more expensive for ordinary buyers.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: electric cars will break the electricity grid
heard_as: The grid can't handle EVs
We don't have enough electricity for EVs
EVs will cause blackouts
Charging will overload the system
The grid isn't ready
We need to build more power plants for EVs
claims.kernel: Because the numbers, if you multiply them naïvely, are terrifying. If every UK driver plugged in at 6:30pm and drew maximum power, peak demand from cars alone would be about **230 GW** — nearly four times the UK's current 60 GW peak. Headlines love this comparison. It just isn't how charging actually works.
claims.truth: Real electricity demand from EVs is much smaller because most cars sit parked most of the time and can charge whenever suits the grid: - **33 million cars** in the UK; average driver does **~20 miles a day** - Most drivers wouldn't need to charge every day — **once a week is often enough** - National Grid estimate: if **all UK cars went electric**, peak demand would rise by **25 to 29%** - All UK **cars, vans and lorries** electric: peak would rise about **40%** - Total annual generation would go from ~300 TWh to about 370 TWh (cars only) or 410 TWh (with vans/lorries) - **The UK was already generating 400 TWh in 2005** — more than would be needed even with every car electric today
claims.say_this: The scary maths only works if you assume every EV charges at the exact same moment, which nobody does. Even if every UK car went electric, the National Grid estimates peak demand would rise about 25 to 29%. That's manageable. With smart charging, EVs can actually help the grid — charging when power is cheap and clean, and even feeding it back when demand spikes.

pushback.if: But everyone will charge at 6pm when they get home.
pushback.reply: Some will, and that would be a problem — which is why smart charging and off-peak tariffs exist. Time-of-use pricing shifts most charging to overnight (or midday for solar owners). Norway is already managing this well, spreading charging across morning, evening and overnight.

pushback.if: The grid can't handle a 30% peak rise.
pushback.reply: Grid capacity grows over time as generation and transmission expand. The UK's peak was **already higher in 2005** than it will be with every car electric today. What made it fall since 2005 was industrial efficiency and appliance efficiency. EVs will lift it back, gradually, in line with grid build-out.

pushback.if: What about extreme weather events, like Texas in winter?
pushback.reply: The Texas grid failed because it was under-invested, not because of EVs. But it points to a real opportunity: **vehicle-to-grid (V2G)** turns cars into a backup source for the grid, exactly for events like that. Germany and the Netherlands are already piloting V2G.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: My one flight makes no difference
heard_as: the plane was going anyway
aviation is only 2% of emissions
they'll have clean fuel soon
claims.kernel: Aviation is a small slice of global emissions, so at the global scale the number really is small. The distribution is what makes the argument fall apart.
claims.truth: Flying is the fastest way for one person to spend their entire annual carbon budget, and it is extremely unequally spread: a small minority of frequent flyers accounts for the large majority of aviation emissions. New Scientist reporting found that high income, environmentally minded people tend to have larger footprints than their peers, mostly because they fly more. The industry's own plan is not on track either. In June 2026 IATA's chief Willie Walsh admitted the 2050 net zero pledge will probably not be achieved, with sustainable aviation fuel sitting at 0.8% of its target.
claims.say_this: Flying is the one choice where a single decision really does move your own number, because most people on earth never fly at all.

pushback.if: Sustainable fuel will fix it
pushback.reply: The head of the airline industry said in 2026 that their 2050 target probably will not be met. Their green fuel is at under 1% of what was planned.

claims.claim: there's no hope for low-carbon flying and shipping
heard_as: You can't decarbonise flying
Shipping is impossible to fix
Aviation will never be clean
We just have to accept flight emissions
There's no green jet fuel
Long-distance travel is stuck with fossil fuels
claims.kernel: Because the physics is unusually unforgiving. A container ship crossing the Pacific carries 80,000 tonnes of cargo for weeks. A jumbo jet lifts hundreds of tonnes to 40,000 feet using enormous amounts of energy per second. Nothing about battery-electric replicates that. Anyone who's read a technical paper on jet fuel replacement knows the shortlist is very small, and none of the options is easy. So "hopeless" feels grounded — until you look at what's actually being tested.
claims.say_this: Aviation and shipping are the hardest sectors to decarbonise, but "hard" isn't "impossible." Norway already runs 60+ electric ferries. Maersk is building 18 methanol-powered container ships. Short flights and ferries can go electric today. For long-haul, we don't yet have a clear winner between hydrogen, biofuels and synthetic fuels — but each has real options being tested. These will probably be the last sectors to fully decarbonise, not sectors that never do.

pushback.if: Battery-electric long-haul flights are impossible.
pushback.reply: Correct — the energy density isn't there and probably won't be for decades. But long-haul isn't the only category, and hydrogen or synthetic fuels can serve it. Battery-electric works for short-haul, which is a real slice of aviation.

pushback.if: Biofuels compete with food.
pushback.reply: Yes, this is a real constraint. Vegetable-oil biofuel for all aviation would use more oil than the world grows for food. Waste-fat biofuel has a much lower ceiling. So biofuels probably handle a share of aviation, not all of it. That's fine — no single fuel is going to solve everything.

pushback.if: Hydrogen aviation needs a fifth of world electricity.
pushback.reply: For **all** current aviation, yes. That's a real scale problem. In practice, hydrogen aviation would grow alongside grid expansion — as more clean electricity comes online, more hydrogen becomes viable. It doesn't need to solve aviation on day one.

pushback.if: Shipping and aviation avoid climate rules.
pushback.reply: True and infuriating. **No country is responsible for international flights or shipping**, so both industries have been able to duck at climate talks for decades. This is a governance problem, not a technology problem. The fix is putting them formally under UN climate accountability.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: Buying local matters more than cutting down on meat
heard_as: food miles are the problem
local beef is fine
it's the transport that does the damage
claims.kernel: Buying local is genuinely good for other reasons: local economies, freshness, seasonal eating, and knowing how your food was produced. It is just not where the carbon is.
claims.truth: Transport is a small share of food emissions overall and almost negligible for the highest impact foods. For beef, transport accounts for well under 1% of the footprint, with nearly all of it coming from land use and methane from the animals themselves. WRI's analysis finds beef uses around 20 times the land and produces around 20 times the emissions of beans per gram of protein. The 2025 EAT-Lancet report found a planetary health diet would cut non CO2 agricultural emissions by 15 to 34%, free up an area of land the size of India, and prevent around 15 million deaths a year. LSHTM and Cornell modelling published in Nature found a healthier global diet could cut land use emissions 85% by 2050.
claims.say_this: What you eat matters far more than how far it travelled. For beef, transport is under 1% of the footprint.

pushback.if: Irish grass fed beef is different
pushback.reply: It is better than feedlot beef on some measures, and still many times the footprint of plants. Less and better is the honest version.

sources.label: WRI, 6 questions about beef and climate

claims.claim: The transition will destroy jobs
heard_as: 40% of US auto jobs will disappear
you're putting whole towns out of work
green jobs don't pay
claims.kernel: There is something real here, and it is not the total. Jobs lost and jobs created are rarely in the same towns, for the same people, at the same time. Dismissing that is how you lose the argument and deserve to.

pushback.if: Tell that to a refinery town
pushback.reply: Completely fair, and that is the argument we should be having. Retraining and regional investment, not pretending the disruption is not real.

claims.claim: heat pumps don't work in cold climates
heard_as: Heat pumps don't work when it's freezing
They stop working below zero
You need a gas backup
They can't heat old houses
Nordics only use them because they're rich
They're a scam in cold climates
claims.kernel: Because it's technically true that heat pumps do lose some efficiency below zero. Every heat pump manufacturer publishes performance curves that show this. Anyone who reads the spec sheet and stops there concludes "yeah, they must struggle." The mistake is treating a small efficiency drop as "doesn't work" rather than "still much better than the alternative."
claims.truth: Heat pump efficiency is measured as **COP (Coefficient of Performance)** — how many units of heat you get out per unit of electricity in. A COP of 3 means 1 kWh of electricity produces 3 kWh of heat. - **Between 5°C and –10°C**, heat pumps average a COP of about **2.7** — solidly efficient - Field study of **550 heat pumps** across Switzerland, Germany, UK, Canada and US: COP ranged from **3.3 in Canada** to **2.5 in China** - Compare to alternatives: - **Gas boiler**: 0.7–0.8 (70–80% efficient — you lose 20–30% up the flue) - **Electric radiator**: ~1.0 - **Heat pump in a UK winter**: ~2.7 — beats both **Real-world users agree.** Nesta surveyed 2,500 UK heat pump users: - **3 out of 4 people** said they were happier, or just as happy, with their heat pump compared to their old heating system - Satisfaction was similar across old Victorian houses and modern homes — so the "doesn't work in old leaky homes" version of the myth also doesn't hold up The countries that have adopted them most: - **Norway, Sweden, Finland**: highest heat pump penetration per household in Europe - **Alaska**: common even with winters below –20°C
claims.say_this: They lose a little efficiency, but they still work. The best proof is that Norway, Sweden and Finland — three of the coldest countries in Europe — have the highest heat pump adoption per household. Alaska is full of them too. If they didn't work in the cold, that wouldn't happen. Real efficiency in a UK winter is around 2.7, still much better than the 0.7 to 0.8 a gas boiler manages.

pushback.if: But they use loads more electricity when it's cold.
pushback.reply: Yes, and that's the honest bit. As the outside temperature drops, COP drops. A UK cold-snap winter day might have a heat pump running closer to COP 2.0 or slightly below. It still beats a gas boiler on energy, though not necessarily on cost (see the [cost myth](heat-pumps-too-expensive.md)).

pushback.if: My old Victorian house won't work with one.
pushback.reply: The Nesta survey found similar satisfaction rates in old and new homes. Good insulation helps everything, but heat pumps do not require perfect insulation. If your radiators are appropriately sized and the installer is competent, an old house works fine.

pushback.if: But badly installed ones don't work well.
pushback.reply: This is the real bottleneck. A poorly installed heat pump underperforms badly. Installing one is a skilled job combining engineering, plumbing, pipe-fitting and refrigeration. The UK has roughly **3,000 trained heat pump engineers** and needs closer to **30,000 by 2030**. Training is the choke point, not the technology.

claims.claim: heat pumps are too expensive
heard_as: You can't afford a heat pump
They only make sense if you're rich
Even with the grant they're too expensive
Running costs are higher than gas
They're a luxury product
Electricity is too expensive for heat pumps to compete
claims.kernel: Because the upfront cheque really is bigger. Households don't think in "lifetime cost" — they think in "what does the installer's quote say." And in the UK, the quote genuinely is £4,500 higher than the boiler alternative even with the grant applied. That's a real barrier, especially for lower-income households. Pretending otherwise doesn't help anyone.
claims.truth: **Upfront cost (UK):** - Heat pump install: about **£12,000** (air-source) - Gas boiler: about **£2,750** (£2,500-£3,000) - Gap: **~£9,000** before grants - **UK government grant**: **£7,500** - **Net gap after grant**: ~**£2,000** more than a gas boiler **The distributional problem is real:** Nesta survey — heat pumps are rare in the poorest UK areas, common among wealthier households. Even at £2,000 above a boiler, they are out of reach for many. **Running cost:** - **UK electricity costs ~4× more than gas** per unit - But heat pumps deliver ~3 units of heat per unit of electricity, so break-even is roughly a COP of 3 - **Average UK heat pump COP: 2.9** — right at the break-even edge Result in the UK today: some households save, some pay more (especially in cold snaps when COP drops). This is not the case globally: - **Average US, European, South Korean and Japanese households saved money on heating by switching in 2021-22** - Continental European savings widened after the Russia-Ukraine gas price spike **Lifetime cost:** - Including install + running over the whole lifespan, heat pumps usually work out **cheaper than a gas boiler** — even in countries where governments pay large subsidies - Heat pumps typically save a few hundred dollars a year on running costs, which recoups the extra upfront over time - Heat pumps are the **cheapest route to decarbonise heating**, cheaper than direct electric heaters or hydrogen boilers
claims.say_this: Running costs are usually lower than a gas boiler, and lifetime cost usually wins too. But the sticker price is genuinely a barrier. In the UK an air-source heat pump is around £12,000 to install versus £2,750 for a gas boiler. Even with the £7,500 government grant, that's still £2,000 more. The problem isn't the technology, it's affordability upfront — which is fixable with bigger grants and fairer electricity pricing.

pushback.if: So they're cheaper only if you can afford the upfront.
pushback.reply: Correct, and this is the specific problem inside the wider claim. **Bigger grants for lower-income households** is the direct policy fix. The current UK grant helps middle-income households but is not enough for low-income ones.

pushback.if: Electricity is 4× the cost of gas in the UK. There's no way it's cheaper to run.
pushback.reply: The efficiency ratio makes up most of that gap. A heat pump at COP 3.0 uses ⅓ the energy of a boiler. 4× cost × ⅓ energy ≈ 1.3× cost — close to break-even. Modern heat pump tariffs from Octopus and OVO can bring the running cost below gas — combining an efficient heat pump with one of these tariffs can **halve** a household's heating bill.

pushback.if: Energy taxes make electricity more expensive than gas.
pushback.reply: Yes, and this is another honest bit of the problem. In many countries, energy taxes are loaded onto electricity rather than gas — historically because gas was assumed to be the household default. Shifting those taxes off electricity, or onto gas instead, would tilt the economics further in favour of heat pumps.
