claims.claim: Heat pumps don't work in cold weather and gas is cheaper anyway
heard_as: they can't heat a house in winter
you need to rip out all your radiators
gas boilers are more efficient
claims.kernel: A badly specified heat pump in a poorly insulated house genuinely does disappoint, and plenty of people have had that experience. Installation quality matters more here than with a boiler.
claims.truth: A heat pump moves heat rather than making it, so it delivers roughly three to five units of heat for every unit of electricity. A gas boiler can never exceed one, because it is limited by the energy in the gas. On cold weather, the countries with the highest heat pump adoption in Europe are the Nordic ones, which settles the physics argument fairly directly. Running cost depends on the local ratio of electricity to gas prices, which is a tax and market design question rather than a technology one.
claims.say_this: A heat pump gives you three to five units of heat per unit of electricity, because it moves heat instead of burning something. Norway and Finland have the highest adoption in Europe.

pushback.if: My neighbour got one and hated it
pushback.reply: Probably a sizing or insulation problem rather than the technology. Bad installs are the single biggest cause of unhappy owners.

claims.claim: My individual actions are a drop in the ocean
heard_as: 100 companies cause 70% of emissions
personal carbon footprints are fossil fuel propaganda
recycling is a distraction
claims.kernel: Arithmetically this is right, and the history backs it up. BP popularised the personal carbon footprint calculator in 2004, and shifting responsibility onto consumers served the industry very well. Someone making this point is not your opponent.
claims.truth: The value of individual action was never the arithmetic of your own tonnes. It is that behaviour is contagious and norms move: research on social tipping points suggests around 25% of a group adopting a behaviour is enough to shift the majority. And the highest impact things an individual does are not really individual at all. How you vote, what you say at work, where your pension and bank put your money, and whether you fly all reach far beyond your own footprint. Worth noting that high income, environmentally concerned people often have larger footprints than their peers, mainly from flying, so attitude on its own does not do it.
claims.say_this: One person recycling changes nothing. One person talking about it, voting on it and moving their pension changes what everyone around them thinks is normal.

pushback.if: It's the corporations, not us
pushback.reply: Agreed, and those corporations respond to regulation and to where money goes. Both of those are things people decide collectively.

claims.claim: what happens when the sun doesn't shine and the wind doesn't blow?
heard_as: What about when the sun doesn't shine?
Renewables are intermittent
You need 100% backup
The grid will fail without fossil fuels
Batteries can't store enough
Renewables are only 30% of the time
We can't rely on the weather
claims.kernel: Because solar and wind really are variable, and if you assume nothing changes about the rest of the grid, "the lights would go out" is the natural conclusion. It's also a favourite argument of fossil fuel commentators, so it gets repeated often. What is usually left out is that grid engineers have been thinking about this since long before renewables existed — the grid always had to match variable demand to variable supply.
claims.truth: There are three time windows to solve, and each has different answers: **1. Minutes to hours (the easy part)** - **Lithium-ion batteries** return about **98% of the electricity** you put in - Very efficient, cheap enough for daily cycles, but not economical for months of storage - Already deployed at grid scale in Australia, California, Texas and elsewhere **2. Hours to days** - **Solar and wind naturally complement each other**: solar peaks in daytime and summer, wind is often stronger at night and in winter - Adding **hydropower, geothermal and nuclear** helps - **Cross-border sharing**: it's always sunny or windy somewhere. Sunny Spain can send power to a cloudy UK, the UK can return the favour when it's windy - Modern high-voltage DC links make this cheap and efficient **3. Weeks to months (the hard part)** Not yet fully solved, but three plausible answers: - **Pumped hydro**: water pumped uphill when power is plentiful, released to generate later. ~80% round-trip efficient. Cheap but geographically constrained. - **Heat storage**: electricity stored as heat in water, rock, sand or molten salt. Useful for industrial heat customers (steel, cement, glass). - **Hydrogen**: electricity makes hydrogen, hydrogen makes electricity later. Only **40-50% efficient** end-to-end — you throw away roughly half the power. But it's storable at scale. **Chris Goodall's cost comparison for two months of UK winter backup:** - Using **batteries alone**: ~**£3 trillion per year** — more than the UK's entire GDP - Using **hydrogen**: billions to tens of billions per year — expensive but manageable Pick the right tool for the timescale. Batteries for short gaps, hydrogen or hydro for long ones. Don't try to use batteries for months of backup.
claims.say_this: This is engineers' oldest question and they've been planning for it from day one. Solar and wind cover each other most of the time — solar peaks in summer and daytime, wind in winter and at night. Batteries cover the minutes-to-hours gap. Cross-border sharing, hydro, geothermal and existing nuclear cover the harder day-to-days. Weeks-to-months is genuinely still being worked out, but hydrogen and heat storage look like the answers.

pushback.if: So it's not solved.
pushback.reply: Short-term is solved. Long-term is being solved — hydrogen and heat storage are demonstrably possible, they just need scaling. The gap in the plan is not "we don't know how", it's "we haven't built it at scale yet." Which is where every energy technology starts.

pushback.if: What if we get a really bad dunkelflaute?
pushback.reply: *Dunkelflaute* — a German term for weeks of low sun and low wind, common in northern European winters — is the specific edge case. It's exactly why hydrogen, biomass, nuclear or gas-with-CCS backup make sense in high-latitude countries. It's a real engineering problem with real solutions. It's not the whole grid, it's the last 5-10%.

pushback.if: You still need gas as backup for renewable systems, so what's the point?
pushback.reply: Some gas as **rare, occasional backup** is much better than gas as **primary generation**. If gas plants only run for 100 hours a year in an emergency instead of 8,760 hours as baseload, emissions fall by orders of magnitude even before the gas plants themselves are replaced with cleaner firm sources.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: Ireland is too small to make any difference
heard_as: we're 0.1% of global emissions
why should we wreck our economy
let the big countries go first
claims.kernel: In absolute terms Ireland is small, and it is reasonable to ask why a small country should move before large ones do.
claims.truth: Small in total, near the top in Europe per person, which is the measure that reflects choices rather than population. The choices here are also not small in scale: Ireland has 107 data centres operating, drawing about 1.3 GW, with EirGrid forecasting they could take 31% of national electricity by 2034. Ireland's data centres already added roughly 360 euro cumulatively to each household's electricity bill between 2015 and 2023. On the wider point, every country emitting under 2% adds up to roughly a third of global emissions, so small equals exempt would exempt a third of the problem.
claims.say_this: Small in total, near the top in Europe per person. And nothing about a third of our electricity going to data centres by 2034 is small.

pushback.if: We should wait for the big emitters
pushback.reply: Everyone under 2% together is about a third of global emissions. If they all wait, a third of the problem never moves.

claims.claim: it's too late, we're heading for 5 or 6 degrees, so nothing matters
heard_as: It's too late anyway
We're already screwed
Nothing we do now matters
We're heading for 5 or 6 degrees regardless
The planet is toast
Doomism
Why bother recycling if we're all doomed
The point of no return has passed
We're cooked
claims.kernel: Because part of it is true. The **1.5°C target is now out of reach**. Even 2°C is unlikely on current form. Anyone still claiming 1.5 is achievable without a miracle is being dishonest, and years of headlines about worst-case scenarios have burned into public memory. If your reference point is Mark Lynas's *Six Degrees* from the mid-2000s, the picture really did look apocalyptic. The despair is grounded in real numbers, and dismissing it as "just doomism" misses the point.
claims.truth: Recent projections narrow the realistic range considerably: - **Current policies (nothing new, nothing better)**: about **2.5 to 3°C** by 2100 (UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2024). - **Countries hit their 2030 targets but do nothing more**: about **2.4°C**. - **Every mid-century net zero pledge is actually delivered**: about **1.8°C**. So the realistic range is roughly **1.8 to 3°C**, not 5 or 6. The extreme scenario often cited in older modelling, labelled **RCP8.5**, is now considered implausible. That does not make 2.5°C safe. It still means most coral reefs lost, worse heatwaves, and serious pressure on food systems, especially in poorer countries. But it is a very different world from the "civilisation collapse" framing, and every fraction of a degree we prevent is a measurable win. There is no single global switch that flips at 1.5 or 2°C.
claims.say_this: The 5 or 6 degree scenarios are not where we are heading any more. Current policies put us at roughly 2.5 to 3 degrees by 2100, and if the net zero pledges are actually delivered, closer to 1.8. That is still a serious, dangerous world, but "too late" is not the same as "nothing matters." Every tenth of a degree we can shave off is a real, measurable win.

pushback.if: 1.5°C is dead, so we've already failed.
pushback.reply: Failing to hit an exact number is not the same as failing on the whole task. 1.7°C is meaningfully better than 1.9°C, which is meaningfully better than 2.1°C. The goal shifts from "hit a specific number" to "cut emissions as fast as possible, whatever number we land near."

pushback.if: We'll hit tipping points and everything collapses anyway.
pushback.reply: Tipping points are real, and they matter for specific systems like the Amazon, the AMOC, and permafrost. They are not one global switch. Passing them makes the case for cutting emissions harder, not weaker, because every degree we prevent lowers the odds of triggering one.

pushback.if: So why bother, if we're still heading for 2.5°C?
pushback.reply: Because 2.5°C is what happens if we drift. 1.8°C is what happens if we actually push. The gap between those two worlds is the difference between coral reefs surviving, food systems coping, and hundreds of millions of people staying in their homes.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: we'll never be able to make low-carbon cement
heard_as: Cement is impossible to decarbonise
You need limestone, so you release CO2, end of story
Cement will always be a climate problem
There's no green cement
We can't replace concrete
claims.kernel: Because the chemistry is uniquely awkward. Cement is made by heating limestone (CaCO3) at very high temperature. Doing that releases CO2 directly from the rock itself — before you even count the fuel used to heat the kiln. There's no way to make cement from limestone without releasing that CO2. If you fix your gaze on that single fact, "cement is impossible to decarbonise" sounds obvious.
claims.truth: **Why cement matters:** - **7% of global greenhouse gas emissions** — more than shipping and aviation combined - For every **1 tonne of concrete**, roughly **1 tonne of CO2** goes into the atmosphere **Three genuine routes to cut it:** **1. Use less cement in concrete.** Cement is one ingredient in concrete (mixed with water, sand, aggregate). Europe's mix is currently ~78% cement. Many countries build safely with much less. Cutting European mixes to 50% cement by 2050 could reduce industry CO2 by **40%**. **2. Carbon capture and storage (CCS).** Capture the CO2 as it leaves the kiln, pipe it underground. This works — **Heidelberg Cement** is building the first commercial-scale plant in Norway. It costs more: - Normal cement: **~$125 per tonne** - CCS-cement: **$100-200 per tonne extra** (75-140% more per Gates' book) - In places with cheap energy: extra cost could be as low as **$40 per tonne** - The US **Inflation Reduction Act** already provides an **$85/tonne tax break** for captured and stored CO2 Even though CCS-cement is expensive per tonne, cement is a small share of what a house costs, so the finished-product impact is **very small**. **3. Use a different rock entirely.** Instead of limestone (which contains carbon), use **calcium silicate rocks like basalt** (which don't). No CO2 released during heating. Useful magnesium by-products can actually **absorb CO2 from the air**. **Brimstone** has proven the concept and is building a test plant. Basalt is one of the most common rocks on Earth.
claims.say_this: Cement is 7% of global emissions and it's the second-most-used material on Earth after water. It's genuinely hard to decarbonise, but there are three real routes and all three work: use less cement in each mix, capture the CO2 at the plant, or use a different rock entirely. The first plant using basalt instead of limestone is being built. Cement made with capture costs more, but adds tiny amounts to the final price of a house.

pushback.if: CCS-cement is way too expensive.
pushback.reply: Per tonne of cement, yes. Per house, the extra cost is tiny — cement is a small fraction of a house's price. And in places with cheap clean energy, the CCS premium can be as low as **$40/tonne**. Government support (like the US IRA's $85/tonne tax credit) closes most of the gap.

pushback.if: Basalt cement is a lab experiment.
pushback.reply: Brimstone has proven the concept and is building a test plant. That's the same stage lab-grown meat was at 10 years ago. Ten years ago most people thought CCS was the only real option. The list has grown.

pushback.if: You can't rebuild every cement plant.
pushback.reply: You don't have to. Use less cement in every mix (route 1) — that alone cuts 40% at zero technology change, only building regulation change. Then retrofit CCS to plants that keep producing (route 2). New capacity in basalt regions can use route 3.

Bill Gates, *How to Avoid a Climate Disaster*

claims.claim: we'll never be able to make low-carbon steel
heard_as: You can't make steel without coal
Steel is impossible to decarbonise
Green steel is a fantasy
It costs too much to compete
There's not enough hydrogen
We'll always need coking coal
claims.kernel: Because two-thirds of the world's steel is made using coal (technically "coke," made from coal). That's been true for over a century — anyone who works in steel knows the coal is central. If you frame the problem as "steel needs coal," decarbonising sounds impossible. What that framing misses is that coal isn't there because steel physically requires it. Coal is there because it strips oxygen out of iron ore. Hydrogen does the same thing without producing CO2.
claims.truth: **Where steel emissions come from:** - **7% of global greenhouse gas emissions** - **~⅔ of the world's steel** is made using coke (from coal); the remaining **⅓** is recycled scrap in electric arc furnaces - 1 tonne of new steel = ~**0.8 tonnes of coal** burned = most of the emissions **Two proven routes to remove coal:** **1. Hydrogen instead of coal.** Hydrogen strips oxygen from iron ore, just like coal does. The by-product is water (H2O), not CO2. Requires clean hydrogen. **2. Direct electrification.** Use electricity instead of burning coal. A third option — **carbon capture** at the current plant — works but is more expensive. **The scale numbers:** - 1 tonne of "green steel" needs **~4 MWh of electricity** - Making the world's 1.3 billion tonnes of steel this way would need **5,200 TWh** — about **⅕ of world electricity generation today** - Total investment needed globally: about **€1.3 trillion**, or **€50 billion/year over 25 years** (per H2 Green Steel figures) **The cost premium is genuinely small on finished products:** - Green steel: **~25% more** per tonne - A $25,000 car: about **$150 more** (0.5-1%) - A $250,000 house: about **$400 more** (0.2%) - An offshore wind turbine: **0.5-2%** cost increase **Who's building it:** - **H2 Green Steel** — plant under construction in Sweden with government support - **ArcelorMittal** — converting a Spanish plant to hydrogen with government support - **Boston Metal** — direct electrification, backed by Microsoft; first plant expected 2026 **Most European steel companies** have committed to cutting emissions **30-50% or more by 2030**.
claims.say_this: We already know how to make green steel — use hydrogen instead of coal, or electrify the process directly. Both are proven at pilot scale and the first commercial plants are being built now in Sweden, Spain and the US. The problem is scale and cost, not technology. Green steel adds about 25% to the price of steel, but that's about $150 on a car and $400 on a house.

pushback.if: Green steel is a lab curiosity.
pushback.reply: Not any more. H2 Green Steel's Boden plant is under construction. Boston Metal's first plant is expected in 2026. ArcelorMittal has committed billions to hydrogen conversion. These are commercial-scale projects, not lab demonstrations.

pushback.if: It needs too much electricity.
pushback.reply: 5,200 TWh globally is about a fifth of current world generation. That's not nothing — but a **25% rise in global electricity demand over 25 years** matches the trajectory of the grid buildout for other electrification (EVs, heat pumps). It's part of the transition, not blocking it.

pushback.if: 25% more expensive means nobody buys it.
pushback.reply: The finished-product impact is tiny. A car maker paying 25% more for its steel raises car prices by less than 1%. Buyers won't notice. What matters is car makers demanding green steel — because their own Scope 3 emissions targets require it.

claims.claim: meat substitutes are too expensive
heard_as: Fake meat is a luxury product
Plant burgers cost twice as much
Vegan food is only for people who can afford it
Lab meat will always be more expensive than real meat
Green food is a rich person's thing
Substitutes aren't at price parity
claims.kernel: Because for some products it's true. Plant-based bacon really does cost more than pork bacon in UK supermarkets. Plant-based burgers can cost noticeably more than beef burgers. Anyone who has bought both knows this. The mistake is generalising "some plant products are pricier" into "plant substitutes are unaffordable" — the picture varies a lot by product.
claims.truth: Looking at **UK supermarket prices per kg**: - **Chicken and plant-based chicken**: overlap heavily; some plant versions are actually cheaper - **Mince**: plant and meat versions overlap in price - **Sausages**: plant and meat versions overlap - **Burgers**: some overlap, but plant burgers can cost noticeably more - **Bacon**: plant-based bacon tends to be more expensive than pork bacon - **Fish**: one of the more expensive meats regardless Overall: plant-based substitutes are not always more expensive, but on average still tend to cost more than the meat equivalent, especially for bacon and burgers. **Lab-grown (cultivated) meat cost trajectory:** - **2013**: about **$2.4 million per kg** - **Today**: roughly **$10-100 per kg** — about **50,000× cheaper** in ~10 years - Cost keeps falling on a curve similar to solar, wind and batteries - Still needs to fall further to compete with chicken; a lot further to compete with cheap beef
claims.say_this: For chicken and mince the price gap is already small — plant versions overlap with meat versions in UK supermarkets. Bacon and burgers still cost more. Lab-grown meat has dropped 50,000× in cost since 2013 and is still falling fast, but it's not yet cheap enough to compete with chicken, let alone beef. Two ways to close the gap: make substitutes cheaper, or make meat reflect its true cost. Cheaper substitutes is the more realistic path.

pushback.if: Just tax meat to level the price.
pushback.reply: Politically extremely hard. UK surveys show **only about 1 in 5 people** support a meat tax. The 2021 UK National Food Strategy consultation found a meat tax was the **least popular idea** among all its suggestions — and it caused strong disagreement among panel members. Meat tax also risks hurting the roughly **3 billion people worldwide who cannot currently afford a full healthy diet**.

pushback.if: Nothing will change unless meat gets more expensive.
pushback.reply: Two paths, not one. Making substitutes cheaper is the more politically viable route. Reallocating **existing farm subsidies away from meat and dairy** toward plant proteins would have a similar price effect to a meat tax, but tends to be more politically acceptable — it's not a new tax, it's just spending public money differently.

pushback.if: Lab-grown meat is a fantasy for the rich.
pushback.reply: At $10-100/kg it's still expensive, but the cost has fallen faster than any food technology in memory. The trajectory looks like solar's — early adopters pay premium prices, then production scaling drops costs steeply. The **regulatory bottleneck** is now more binding than the cost bottleneck. Singapore and the US have approved cultivated meat for humans; the UK allows it only for pet food; Italy and some US states have banned it outright.

Impossible Burger is basically Coke
You should just eat vegetables, not processed alternatives
claims.kernel: Because "ultra-processed" as a category has a bad reputation, and rightly so — high consumption is linked to obesity, diabetes, cancer and heart disease. If plant-based meats meet the technical definition of ultra-processed, it's easy to lump them in. The mistake is treating "ultra-processed" as one homogeneous category when the evidence shows the harm comes from specific sub-groups (processed meats, sugary drinks), not from all processed food equally.
claims.truth: **Nutrition compared to processed meat:** - Meat substitutes tend to have **fewer calories, less total fat, less saturated fat** - Usually **higher in fibre** - Some match a beef burger's 20-25 g protein per serving; some come in lower at ~15 g - Protein **quality** is worth noting: animal foods contain the full range of amino acids; plant foods often need combining (a varied plant diet does it easily) - Substitutes often fall short on **calcium, zinc and vitamin B12** unless fortified — many products are now fortified **The "ultra-processed" checklist** (typical criteria — 8 markers): | Criteria | Processed meat | Plant-based meat | |---|---|---| | Convenient | ✅ | ✅ | | High in calories | ✅ | ❌ | | High in sugar | ❌ | ❌ | | High in saturated fat | ✅ | ❌ | | High in salt | ✅ | ❌ | | Many ingredients | ✅ | ✅ | | Low in fibre | ✅ | ❌ | | Couldn't be made in a normal kitchen | ✅ | ✅ | Plant-based meat ticks **3 of 8** markers. Processed meat ticks **6 of 8**. Not the same category on any measure that actually matters for health. **What the health evidence actually says:** - High **overall** ultra-processed food consumption is linked to obesity, diabetes, cancer, heart disease - When researchers look inside the "UPF" category, the food groups doing the damage are **processed meats and sugary drinks** - Other UPFs, including meat substitutes, **show no link to higher disease risk** — some studies even find **lower risk** - More **plant-based protein** in the diet is associated with better health outcomes and lower early-death risk
claims.say_this: They tick some ultra-processed boxes — many ingredients, factory-made — but they miss the ones that actually cause harm: high calories, high saturated fat, high salt, low fibre. In the health evidence, the ultra-processed foods clearly linked to disease are **processed meats** and **sugary drinks**. Plant-based meats don't show the same link, and some studies find they're associated with lower disease risk. Grouping veggie burgers with fizzy drinks isn't supported by the science.

pushback.if: But they're still ultra-processed.
pushback.reply: Yes, technically. But the "ultra-processed" category is heterogeneous. A veggie burger and a can of Coke both meet the definition, but they behave very differently in the body. The specific health harms come from calorie density, saturated fat, salt, low fibre, and specific ingredients like nitrates in processed meat. Meat substitutes don't hit those harm markers.

pushback.if: Cows are natural, factories aren't.
pushback.reply: Naturalness isn't a nutritional metric. A beef burger and a plant burger both come out of a factory to a large extent (mince, stabilisers, packaging). The question is what's inside them, not where they were assembled.

pushback.if: What about processing damaging the food?
pushback.reply: Fair concern. Some processing does affect nutrition — very high heat, very long processing, chemical solvents. Modern extrusion and mycoprotein processes retain most nutritional value, though not all. If you're worried, tofu, tempeh and unprocessed legumes are the base-line reference — cheaper and healthier than most substitutes, though less convenient.

claims.claim: meat substitutes are worse for the climate because they're processed
heard_as: Beyond Meat is worse than a real steak
Processed food has a bigger footprint
The energy in fake meat cancels the benefit
Lab-grown meat is worse than beef
Impossible Burgers aren't really green
Factory food is climate-heavy
claims.kernel: Because factory-made food does use energy — running fermenters, heating, packaging, refrigerated logistics — and that shows up as emissions. It sounds intuitive that "grown naturally on a farm" would be lower carbon than "manufactured in a factory." What that intuition misses is how much land use and methane emissions come from actual livestock production, which is much bigger than any factory energy input.
claims.truth: Ritchie compares carbon emissions **per 100 g of protein**, whole supply chain (farming, processing, packaging): - **Beef and lamb** are by far the highest-emitting protein sources on the planet - **Pork** is lower than beef/lamb but still very high - **Meat substitutes** (Impossible Burger, Beyond Meat, tofu, Quorn/mycoprotein, peas) all cause **much lower emissions than beef and lamb** — often **more than 10× lower than pork** - Meat substitutes also beat **most chicken and egg production** — only the most efficient chicken farms come close - **Lab-grown (cultivated) meat**: lower than beef, roughly similar to chicken - Even when comparing substitutes to the **most climate-friendly beef and pork farmers** (not the average), substitutes still win almost every time - Straight plant foods (**peas, beans, lentils**) still beat processed substitutes, but the substitutes still beat any meat
claims.say_this: They're not. Meat substitutes use energy in factories, but they still cause much less carbon than real meat, especially beef and lamb — often more than ten times less than pork. Even compared to the most climate-friendly beef farms, substitutes come out ahead almost every time. Peas and beans still beat processed substitutes, but the substitutes still comfortably beat any meat.

pushback.if: But they use so much electricity to make.
pushback.reply: They do — and it's still nothing next to methane from ruminants. Livestock emissions are dominated by methane (from cow digestion) and land-use change (from clearing forest for pasture). Factory energy for a plant burger is a small addition compared to what a cow burps out over its life.

pushback.if: But I read lab-grown meat could be 25× worse than beef.
pushback.reply: That headline came from a **specific study using a biopharmaceutical-style production method** — an unusual, energy-intensive way of making lab meat, not how the industry actually plans to do it. Standard cultivated-meat processes are much lower carbon than beef, even when run on today's fossil-heavy grid. If they run on solar or wind, they're dramatically better.

pushback.if: Are substitutes really better than the best beef?
pushback.reply: Yes, in almost every case. Even the most climate-efficient beef producers still emit more per 100 g of protein than a plant burger does. The gap between "best beef" and "average beef" is real, but both sit above substitutes.

claims.claim: we'll just swap fossil fuel dependency for mineral dependency
heard_as: We'd just depend on China instead of the Middle East
Rare earths are the new oil
It's a bad trade — one dependency for another
China controls the transition
Mineral dependency is worse than fossil fuel dependency
We're going to get held hostage by Beijing
claims.kernel: Because the concentration numbers really are stark. China dominates rare earth refining, cobalt production is heavily DRC-centred, lithium is concentrated in Australia and South America. If you frame this as "we'd depend on China for energy instead of Saudi Arabia," it sounds like trading one dependency for another. What that framing misses is that fossil dependency is on the running of the system, whereas mineral dependency is on the building of it.
claims.truth: **Mining concentration:** - **>70% of cobalt** is mined in the DRC - **>60% of rare earths and graphite** are produced in China - **>70% of platinum** comes from South Africa **Refining concentration (even more concentrated):** - China refines **>80% of world rare earths** - China also dominates refining of cobalt, lithium and copper - China dominates finished-product production too: **batteries and EVs** **Fossil fuel dependency for comparison:** - **86% of the world's population** live in countries that **import fossil fuels** (energy insecure) - Only **14%** live in fossil fuel exporters - When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, **up to 50,000 people across Europe died** from cold + energy poverty; high energy prices also pushed food prices up (via fertiliser costs) **Renewables shift the picture dramatically:** - If the world ran on renewables, **92% of the world's population** would live in countries with enough sun or wind to cover **at least 10× their own energy needs** - Only **8%** would have marginal renewable resources
claims.say_this: There's a real concentration in mineral supply — China refines 80% of the world's rare earths, the DRC mines 70% of cobalt. But this is a different kind of risk than fossil fuel dependency. Fossil fuels are fuels: cut off the supply and the lights go out. Minerals are used to build things: cut off supply and you can't build **new** clean tech, but the panels and turbines you already have keep working. Nobody can turn off the sun.

pushback.if: So we'd just be dependent on China instead of Saudi Arabia.
pushback.reply: For the near-term build-out, partially yes. But once you have solar panels and turbines installed, nobody can cut off the sun or the wind. Fossil fuels require an unbroken supply chain forever. Minerals require a supply chain for the build-out phase only.

pushback.if: China could weaponise rare earths.
pushback.reply: They already tried, briefly, in the 2010 dispute with Japan. Prices spiked and the world responded by finding non-Chinese sources. Reserves and refining capacity outside China grew fast. Rare earth cartelisation is much harder than oil cartelisation because rare earths are geologically widespread — they just aren't refined widely.

pushback.if: But we still need to build a lot for decades.
pushback.reply: Yes. That's why the diversification push matters. **US, Australia, Norway, Sweden, Portugal** are all developing new mining and refining capacity. Norway recently discovered Europe's largest rare-earth deposit. The **US Inflation Reduction Act** is putting significant money into domestic mineral processing. AI-driven mineral discovery (KoBold Metals, HyperSpectral) is making new deposits easier to find. This is a solvable diversification problem, not a dependency trap.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: There aren't enough minerals in the world to build all this
heard_as: we'll run out of lithium
there isn't enough copper for the grid
peak minerals
claims.kernel: Clean technology genuinely is more mineral intensive. The IEA notes a typical electric car needs about six times the mineral inputs of a conventional one, and an onshore wind plant about nine times more than a gas plant.
claims.truth: More intensive is not the same as impossible. The Energy Transitions Commission found no fundamental shortage of key materials, with known geological resources exceeding projected demand out to 2050. Critical mineral demand roughly triples by 2030, to around 30 million tonnes a year, set against roughly 15 billion tonnes of fossil fuels extracted every year now. A 2023 study in Joule put total demand to 2050 at up to 1.96 billion tonnes of steel, 241 million tonnes of aluminium and 82 million tonnes of copper, small fractions of accessible reserves, and found annual production need not grow by more than 20% for supply to meet demand. Unlike coal, these materials can be recovered and used again.
claims.say_this: We dig up about 15 billion tonnes of fossil fuel every year and set fire to it. The transition needs around 30 million tonnes of minerals a year, and you can use those again.

pushback.if: But the mines don't exist yet
pushback.reply: That is the real constraint, and it is about permitting and investment timelines, not geology. Worth arguing about. Different argument though.

IEA, critical minerals in clean energy transitions

claims.claim: All that mining is worse for the planet than fossil fuels
heard_as: child labour in cobalt mines
lithium mining destroys the environment
it's just swapping one extraction for another
claims.kernel: Mining causes real environmental and social harm, including water use, habitat loss and serious human rights abuses in some supply chains. Anyone raising this deserves to be told they are right about that part.
claims.truth: The comparison still does not hold. Even counting waste rock, the energy transition involves less material extraction than today's fossil fuel economy does. The decisive difference is that it is a one time build: a wind turbine's materials are dug up once, installed, and can later be recycled, whereas coal, oil and gas must be extracted and burned continuously, forever. Fossil fuel extraction is also not exactly clean or free of human rights problems, it is just older and less discussed.
claims.say_this: Mining does real harm and that should be fixed. The difference is you mine for a turbine once, and you mine for a coal plant every single day it runs.

pushback.if: So you accept the harm as long as it's green
pushback.reply: No. Push for traceable supply chains and recycling. That fight is worth having and it is not an argument for burning more gas meanwhile.

claims.claim: there isn't enough clean energy to replace fossil fuels
heard_as: Renewables can't replace fossil fuels
There isn't enough solar and wind to power the world
The sun doesn't shine at night
It's physically impossible to run everything on renewables
We'd need to cover the whole planet in solar panels
Clean energy is too small to matter
claims.kernel: Because the numbers, at first glance, look enormous. The world uses hundreds of exajoules of energy every year. If someone tells you all of that has to be replaced by solar panels and wind turbines, it sounds impossible in any human timescale. The mistake is measuring the target in "primary energy" — the total energy input including everything that gets wasted as heat. That measure is designed for a world that burns fuel, not one that runs on electricity.
claims.truth: Burning fuel is astonishingly wasteful, and the alternative is much more efficient: - A **coal power plant** turns about **one third** of its energy into electricity; the rest is heat lost up the chimney. **Gas power** wastes about half. Solar and wind waste almost nothing. - Therefore **1 unit of solar or wind can replace 2 to 3 units of coal**. A city needing 100 TWh of electricity would burn 300 TWh of coal to get it, or 200 TWh of gas, or just 100 TWh of solar and wind. - **Petrol cars are only about 20% efficient** — 80 cents of every €1 of petrol becomes waste heat. **Electric cars are about 80% efficient**. Driving an EV uses **only a quarter to a third of the energy** of a petrol car. - If the world electrified everything that can be electrified (cars, heating, industry, short flights, ferries), **total world energy demand would fall by around 40%**, from about **416 EJ today to about 247 EJ** (Ritchie 2024) — even as electricity demand rises. - Renewables are already doing most of the new work: between **2010 and 2022, renewables supplied 57% of the growth** in global electricity, and in **2022 alone they supplied 92%** of new demand.
claims.say_this: We don't need to build clean energy to match our current fossil fuel use, one-for-one. That's the wrong target. Because burning fuel wastes most of the energy it makes, one unit of solar or wind can replace two to three units of coal. If we electrify what we currently burn — cars, heating, industry — total world energy demand actually falls by about 40%, even as electricity demand goes up.

pushback.if: But electricity demand is going up, that proves it isn't working.
pushback.reply: Rising electricity demand is exactly what you would expect if the transition is working. Cars, heat pumps and industry are moving off gas and petrol and onto the grid. **Total** energy demand is what falls. Electricity is the visible tip of a much bigger and mostly hidden efficiency gain.

pushback.if: OK, but poor countries will need much more energy as they develop.
pushback.reply: Yes, and that is right and fair. Rich countries will use less; poorer countries will use more; the world total still falls, because the switch away from burning is such a large efficiency win. The two things are not in conflict.

pushback.if: You're leaving out storage — solar and wind are intermittent.
pushback.reply: Not entirely. The **first 70 to 80% of a power system** can be covered by solar and wind plus modest storage. The **last 20 to 30%** is harder in regions with poor sun and wind, and needs other tools — nuclear, hydro, geothermal, batteries, gas as a decreasing backup. That is a real engineering problem, but it is very different from "there isn't enough clean energy at all."

claims.claim: there aren't enough EV chargers
heard_as: There are no chargers where I live
I can never find a working charger
Charging is a nightmare
The infrastructure isn't there
It's not built out enough yet
You can't rely on public chargers
Rural areas are being left behind
claims.kernel: Because in a lot of specific places it is true. If you live in a city apartment with no off-street parking and the nearest public charger is a mile away, is often broken, or is charging petrol prices, "there aren't enough chargers" is not paranoia. Surveys of over 31,000 EV drivers across 15 countries keep finding charger availability as their top concern, and **41% of would-be buyers say they'd only switch if chargers were as easy to find as petrol stations**.
claims.truth: - **Over a million public charging points** are being installed globally every year - **EU charging network tripled in three years** and is ahead of its own targets - Global average in 2023: **10 EVs per public charger** — but that number hides huge variation: - **New Zealand: 88 EVs per charger** (thin infrastructure) - **South Korea: 3 EVs per charger** (dense infrastructure) - The EV-per-charger metric misses two things: **how fast** each charger delivers (a fast charger serves more cars per day than a slow one), and **where people actually charge** (most charge at home) Home charging patterns matter more than public numbers suggest: - **Only ~5% of Americans** rely mainly on public chargers - **UK: ~20%** rely mainly on public - **UK: 70% of homes have off-street parking** where they could charge — but **only 30% of city EV drivers** have that option - **~30% of UK drivers charge at work** Even the oil industry is joining in: **Shell** and others are installing chargers at their own petrol stations.
claims.say_this: Depends where you live. Some countries have plenty and are building fast. Others are behind. Globally, over a million public chargers are being installed every year, the EU tripled its network in three years, and even oil companies like Shell are adding chargers to petrol stations. The real problem is targeting the places that don't have home charging, and keeping the chargers working reliably.

pushback.if: There are barely any chargers on the motorway.
pushback.reply: Depends on the country. In much of Western Europe, motorway rapid chargers are now common. In North America and the UK the gaps are smaller than they were three years ago. Where the network is thin, that's a real problem — and the fix is targeted infrastructure investment.

pushback.if: Half the ones I've tried are broken.
pushback.reply: Reliability is the specific problem inside the wider problem. Number of chargers installed matters less than percentage of chargers actually working. Some networks are notorious for downtime. Regulation on uptime and payment interoperability is the fix, not more construction.

pushback.if: I live in a flat with no driveway, and rapid chargers are expensive.
pushback.reply: The clearest inequality in the EV story. Fixing it needs **street-side and neighbourhood charging** for people without garages, at prices closer to home-charging cost, not rapid-charger cost. It is a policy problem, not a physics problem.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: there isn't enough land for everyone to go plant-based
heard_as: There isn't enough land for everyone to eat plants
Vegan diets would need more land
We can't grow enough vegetables for everyone
Grazing land would go to waste
The math doesn't work for a plant-based world
Cows use land we can't use anyway
claims.kernel: Because at first glance, replacing meat with lots of vegetables sounds like you'd need lots of extra veg fields. There's also a common intuition that grazing land is "wasted" if it's not producing meat — so switching away from meat would somehow strand it. The mistake is missing that most of the cropland today is already growing food for animals, not people.
claims.truth: **Where farmland actually goes:** - **Grazing land + cropland used for animal feed = 75% of all farmland on Earth** - Only **half of the world's cereal crops** go directly to human food - **75% of the world's soybeans are fed to animals**, not humans - **Tofu, tempeh, soy milk use only 7% of world soy** (~20% including soybean oil) **How wasteful animals are as calorie converters:** - Feed a **cow** 100 calories → get **3 calories** back as meat or milk - Feed a **pig** 100 calories → get 9 back - Feed a **chicken** 100 calories → get 13 back Animals give us about **37% of our calories** but eat most of the crops. **What a plant-shift means for land** (from the modelling Ritchie cites): - **Current diet**: about **4 billion hectares** of farmland - **Fully plant-based diet**: about **1 billion hectares** - That's a **75% cut** The reason grazing land doesn't fully help even if released: **two-thirds of the world's grazing land can't grow crops anyway** — the soil, terrain or climate isn't suitable. So it isn't waste, but it also can't easily be turned into cropland.
claims.say_this: The opposite. Going more plant-based needs less land, not more, because most farmland today grows food for animals, not for people. Three-quarters of the world's farmland supports livestock. A fully vegan world would need about **1 billion hectares** of cropland instead of the current 4 billion — a 75% drop. Even a moderate shift makes a bigger difference than a few people going fully vegan.

pushback.if: But what about the land the animals graze on?
pushback.reply: Two-thirds of it can't grow crops anyway. That's fine — grazing is a legitimate use of unarable land. The issue is the **arable land** that today grows soy and maize to feed animals, when it could grow food for humans directly. That share is the big saving.

pushback.if: Everyone going vegan is unrealistic.
pushback.reply: Correct, and Ritchie is explicit about this. She doesn't argue for 100% vegan. Even a moderate cut in meat and dairy across the whole world would matter more than a small group of people going fully vegan. That's the target, not a plant-only future.

pushback.if: You'd need vast new fields of vegetables.
pushback.reply: Some, yes — more fruit and vegetables would be needed. But the drop in animal-feed cropland is much larger, so the net effect is much less total farmland used. This is the [EAT-Lancet](../sectors/agriculture-food/eat-lancet-planetary-diet-2025.md) modelling number: total agricultural land falls by about 3.4 million km² — an area the size of India — under a full dietary shift.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: there isn't enough public support to tackle climate change
heard_as: Nobody cares about climate change any more
The public won't accept it
There's no political will
People say they care but they don't act
Everyone's too busy with the cost of living to care about climate
Support has collapsed since the pandemic
It's a niche issue
claims.kernel: Because the media environment makes it feel like nobody agrees on anything. Every news cycle features a fresh climate protest and a fresh backlash, an oil-industry lobbyist and a Greta Thunberg quote, a viral tweet from a climate denier and another from a climate doomer. If your only exposure is X, cable news or partisan headlines, it looks like a 50-50 shouting match. Politicians and industry executives repeat this framing because it is convenient: if the public is split, doing nothing is a defensible position.
claims.truth: Multiple large international surveys keep finding overwhelming, cross-country majorities in favour of climate action: - **63-country survey (59,000 people)**: **86% think humans are causing climate change** and see it as a serious threat. Nearly three quarters back specific policies — carbon taxes, more public transport, renewables, EV chargers, airline taxes. - **125-country survey (130,000 people)**: **89% want more political action**. **86% think people in their country should try to fight climate change**. - **United States** (often assumed to be the outlier): **74%** think the US should join international climate action; **71%** say climate change is already causing harm to Americans. - **European Union**: **93%** see climate change as a serious problem; over two-thirds think their government is not doing enough. - Across countries, the share who want their government to do more ranges from **97% in China down to 62% in Finland**. **Most countries land above 80%**. The **perception gap** is the real story. When asked to estimate how many others support climate action, people consistently guess about half the real number. Americans guessed roughly a third supported climate action, versus the real figure of around two thirds. Climate supporters think they are the minority. They are, in fact, the majority almost everywhere.
claims.say_this: Most people, in every country surveyed, want climate action. Around 86% of people worldwide agree humans are causing climate change, and about 89% want more political action. The catch is that almost everyone underestimates how many others agree with them. Americans guess a third of their countrymen support climate action; the real number is closer to two thirds. The silent majority thinks it is the minority. That is fixable.

pushback.if: If people really supported action, they'd vote for it.
pushback.reply: They often do, and the party landscape mostly does not reflect the size of the majority. Perception gap and party alignment are two separate problems. In elections where climate is on the ballot as a specific proposal, it usually wins (California, several EU referenda). Where it is bundled with other issues, party loyalty dominates and the climate question is hard to read from the result.

pushback.if: Support is one thing, willingness to pay is another.
pushback.reply: Fair, and this is one of the real tensions. But the surveys also test willingness to accept specific policies (carbon taxes, airline levies, home retrofits) and majorities remain — especially where the policy is designed to protect lower-income households. What people reject is being asked to pay while a small number at the top pay nothing.

pushback.if: The US is different.
pushback.reply: Less than you think. **74% of Americans support the US joining international climate action**; **71% say Americans are already being harmed by climate change**. What is unusual about the US is not the level of public support, it is the gap between public opinion and political outcomes.

claims.claim: nuclear power takes too long to build to matter for the climate
heard_as: Nuclear is too slow to matter
It's already too late for nuclear
Solar is faster and cheaper
Hinkley Point proves nuclear is impossible
By the time it's built the climate crisis will be worse
We don't have time for nuclear
claims.kernel: Because the Western examples are shockingly bad. **Hinkley Point C** in the UK started construction in 2017; it now looks unlikely to produce power before 2031 — at least **14 years** for the first unit. **Flamanville** in France started in 2007 and only opened in 2024 — more than a **decade late**. Both are terrible advertisements for nuclear power at exactly the moment climate policy needs speed. Anyone looking at those two projects and concluding "nuclear is too slow" is being reasonable.
claims.truth: The Western examples are outliers, not the global norm. Looking at data on over 600 nuclear plants built since 1950: - Around **80% took less than a decade** to build - **1 in 5 took less than 5 years** - Global average construction time: **6 to 8 years** Where is the speed today? - **China and South Korea** are currently building at about **5-7 years per plant** - **India** is building too, more slowly - Nearly all US and EU plants are **>30 years old** — those countries essentially stopped building. When you restart from cold, everything is slow. Why the West is slow (Ritchie's diagnosis): 1. **Plants aren't repeated.** Almost every Western plant is a bespoke design. No learning curve. 2. **Regulations shift mid-build.** Design changes partway through cost enormous amounts of time and money. 3. **Skilled workforce gone.** The UK and France stopped building; the expertise left with the retirements. 4. **Big complex construction projects generally overrun.** Nuclear is on the harder end of that class.
claims.say_this: Nuclear plants in the West often take over a decade because we haven't built any for 30 years and had to relearn how. Countries that keep building regularly — China, South Korea, India — do it in five to eight. Nuclear won't outrun solar and wind, but calling it "too slow" reflects the recent Western experience, not what's physically possible.

pushback.if: Solar and wind are faster to build, why bother with nuclear?
pushback.reply: They are, and most new capacity will be renewable. But grids in high-latitude countries with poor winter sun still need firm low-carbon backup, and nuclear is one of the few options. It's a partner to solar and wind, not a competitor.

pushback.if: The Hinkley Point disaster proves the whole industry is broken.
pushback.reply: Hinkley is a bad advertisement, but it isn't representative. It's a first-of-its-kind design in a country that hadn't built for 20 years. The lesson is not "nuclear is impossible" — it's "build the same design many times in a row, keep regulations stable, and keep the workforce employed between projects."

pushback.if: We don't have time to wait 8 years.
pushback.reply: An 8-year build starting today finishes in the mid-2030s. That is still useful. Better yet: renewables handle the near-term growth while nuclear plants under construction come online to backfill the retiring fossil fleet.

claims.claim: nuclear power is too dangerous
heard_as: Nuclear is dangerous
Remember Chernobyl / Fukushima
One accident would kill millions
Nuclear radiation causes cancer
We can't take the risk
The people who lived near Fukushima are all sick
claims.kernel: Because Chernobyl and Fukushima are burned into public memory, and any nuclear accident is dramatic, one-off, image-heavy. Chernobyl became a Netflix series. Fossil fuel deaths happen quietly, spread out, 11,000 to 22,000 people every single day from air pollution — and there's no headline for that. Anyone whose reference point is the drama of the accidents will overweight nuclear's real risk.
claims.truth: Deaths per terawatt-hour of electricity generated (Markandya & Wilkinson, Sovacool, UNSCEAR): | Energy source | Deaths per TWh | |---|---| | Brown coal | 33 | | Coal | 25 | | Gas | 2.8 | | Hydro | 1.3 | | Wind, Solar, Nuclear | <0.1 each | - Nuclear causes **>99% fewer deaths than coal** and **~98% fewer than gas**. - Wind, nuclear and solar are all so close in the data that we can't confidently rank them — but all three are dramatically safer than fossil fuels. That's the point. The two big disasters, honestly counted: - **Three Mile Island (1979, level 5)**: zero deaths. - **Fukushima (2011, level 7)**: no one died directly in the disaster. About 40-50 injuries. One later cancer death (disputed). Around **2,313 premature deaths from the evacuation** (elderly displacement, healthcare disruption). Total ~2,314. Wider-population cancer studies find no measurable increase. - **Chernobyl (1986, level 7)**: confirmed direct toll under 100. A reasonable broader estimate is **300 to 500 deaths**. Higher WHO figures (up to 4,000 long-term) are now considered too high; UNSCEAR follow-ups found no solid evidence of higher cancer rates in the wider population. Even taking the highest figure (4,000 across all nuclear history), coal air pollution kills more people every single week.
claims.say_this: Nuclear power isn't risk-free, but it is one of the safest energy sources we have. Per unit of electricity, it kills fewer people than coal or gas by a factor of hundreds, and it's roughly on par with solar and wind. The fear is much bigger than the actual risk. What is dangerous is the fossil fuel system nuclear could displace — that quietly kills 4 to 8 million people a year through air pollution.

pushback.if: You can't compare a rare huge accident with steady day-to-day deaths.
pushback.reply: You can and you have to. Both are real. Fossil fuel deaths are not less real because they happen quietly. If your decision framework only counts dramatic events, you end up preferring the system that kills more people overall.

pushback.if: What about the next Chernobyl?
pushback.reply: A future accident is not impossible, especially as more plants get built. The right response is safer reactor designs and sensible siting, not sticking with fossil fuels — which are quietly killing millions today.

pushback.if: Nuclear plants are terrorism targets.
pushback.reply: Modern containment structures are extremely hard to breach. Water reservoirs behind hydro dams are also potentially catastrophic if attacked. The response is security, not abandonment.

claims.claim: nuclear power is too expensive
heard_as: Nuclear is uneconomic
Hinkley Point C cost £30 billion
Solar is way cheaper
You'd never build nuclear if you had to compete
Nuclear only survives on subsidies
Nobody would invest in nuclear without government backing
claims.kernel: Because the Western numbers are eye-watering. **US Vogtle 3 and 4** is expected to cost at least **$6,000 per kilowatt** — a sixfold jump from 1960s US plants at ~$1,000/kW. **Hinkley Point C** in the UK is one of the most expensive infrastructure projects in British history. Meanwhile, solar and wind have dropped 80-90% over the same period. Anyone comparing headline Western nuclear numbers against a solar farm bid concludes that nuclear can't compete.
claims.truth: Cost per megawatt built since 2000 (Britain Remade / Dumitriu & Hopkinson data, £m per MW): | Country | £m per MW | |---|---| | South Korea | £2.24 | | India | £2.26 | | China | £2.37 | | Japan | £2.67 | | France | £4.43 | | Finland | £5.97 | | UK | £9.42 | | USA | £10.23 | **The US and UK are 4-5 times more expensive than South Korea.** Wages in the UK and South Korea are similar, so labour cost differences don't explain a fivefold gap. What does explain it: 1. **Projects run late; delays cost money.** Labour is ~80% of typical cost overruns on delayed nuclear projects. 2. **Regulations keep changing.** Design changes mid-build cascade through the whole project. 3. **Plants aren't built repeatedly.** The US has ~50 reactors, nearly all decades old. The US DOE estimates you'd need to build **at least 20 identical plants** to work out the real steady-state cost. That hasn't happened.
claims.say_this: Nuclear is expensive in the US and UK — no argument. But South Korea builds nuclear plants for about a fifth of the US price, and China and India are close. The cost is not inherent to nuclear; it comes from stop-start construction, changing regulations and bespoke designs. Where countries build consistently, they build cheaply.

pushback.if: Solar and wind are much cheaper. Why bother?
pushback.reply: They are, and most new capacity will be renewable. But grids in high-latitude countries need firm low-carbon backup. **The first 70-80% of a grid from solar and wind is cheap; the last 20-30% is expensive**, especially through winter with little sun and wind. In that last slice, a mix of nuclear + storage might end up cheaper than solar/wind + massive long-duration storage alone.

pushback.if: Once built, isn't it also expensive to run?
pushback.reply: No — **running costs are low**. Fuel is a small share of nuclear costs; the plant produces power for 40-60 years once built. Fossil fuel plants keep buying fuel for the life of the plant. The high-cost bit is construction, not operations.

pushback.if: The West has proven it can't do this cheaply.
pushback.reply: Currently, yes. But that's a consequence of decades of not building. South Korea and China have shown you can build in the £2-3m/MW range. The fixes are consistency, standardisation and a stable regulatory environment.

claims.claim: nuclear waste is an unsolved problem
heard_as: We don't know what to do with nuclear waste
Nuclear waste stays radioactive for millions of years
There's no safe place to store it
We're leaving a problem for our grandchildren
Yucca Mountain proves we can't solve this
One leak would be catastrophic
claims.kernel: Because "we haven't built a permanent storage site yet" is a real statement. Countries have talked about deep geological storage for decades, and until Finland's Onkalo opens, nobody can point at a working example. That gap between intention and execution feels like a hole in the safety case. It's a fair concern — just a different one from "we don't know what to do."
claims.truth: Nuclear waste is not one thing. It's split into three categories, by volume and by radioactivity: | Type | Share of volume | Share of radioactivity | |---|---|---| | Low-level (gloves, tools) | 92% | 1% | | Intermediate-level | 7% | 4% | | High-level (used fuel rods) | 1% | 95% | - **Low-level waste** (mostly used gloves, mops, tools) is not very radioactive. It's stored near-surface in concrete vaults for ~100 years and mostly decays away in decades. - **Intermediate-level waste** needs longer isolation in multi-layered casks. - **High-level waste** is the small but serious 1% — mostly used fuel rods, holding 95% of the radioactivity. The good news on high-level waste: - **Up to 96% of the material can be recycled** back into fresh nuclear fuel. Countries doing this: France, Japan, Russia, China. Not doing it: the US, wasting a large potential energy source. - Small volume: **~29,000 m³ of high-level waste worldwide by 2016**. Piled on a football pitch, that would be **~5 metres high** — tiny compared to fossil fuel waste. - **Zero deaths or injuries** have ever been caused by nuclear waste storage. - Nuclear is **the most regulated and monitored waste industry in the world**. - **Coal ash contains mercury, arsenic, lead, cadmium and chromium** — and is often more radioactive than well-managed nuclear waste — but gets a fraction of the attention.
claims.say_this: We already know how to store nuclear waste safely — deep underground, in rock tested for stability. What we haven't done at scale yet is prove it in practice. Finland is about to. Nuclear waste is small in volume (all high-level waste ever produced would fit on a football pitch, 5 metres high), zero people have ever died from it, and much of it can be recycled. The public worry is bigger than the physical problem.

pushback.if: But no country has actually built a permanent underground site.
pushback.reply: **Finland has.** The **Onkalo repository** is 430 metres deep, in rock tested for stability, designed to keep waste isolated for at least 100,000 years. It's expected to open in the next few years. That is the real-world test. If Onkalo works, others follow with more confidence and a real cost benchmark.

pushback.if: But the US Yucca Mountain site failed.
pushback.reply: Yes. Yucca Mountain took decades and was cancelled, mostly for political reasons. That is a failure of policy, not of the underlying physics. Finland succeeded because it managed the local political process well from the start.

pushback.if: 100,000 years is a long time to guarantee safety.
pushback.reply: It is, and this is where scientists genuinely disagree. Direct radiation exposure becomes safe within ~1,000 years. If waste ever contaminated water or food, some isotopes remain dangerous much longer — estimates range from 10,000 to 1,000,000 years. Deep geological sites are designed conservatively, to buffer the extreme end of that range.

claims.claim: poor countries need fossil fuels to develop
heard_as: Africa needs coal
Poor countries need fossil fuels to lift people out of poverty
It's colonial to deny them development
You can't be green when you're poor
The West did it, so should they
Energy justice means fossil fuels
claims.kernel: Because for 100 years it was true. Every country that industrialised did so on coal, oil and gas. Nobody had a serious alternative. There is also a real fairness argument buried in the claim: rich countries burned fossil fuels for centuries to get where they are, then turned around and told poorer countries not to. That hypocrisy is real, and people are right to be suspicious when it comes wrapped in climate messaging.
claims.truth: The premise, that fossil fuels are the necessary fuel for development, is no longer accurate. Fossil fuels **were** the fuel; **energy in general** is what lifts people out of poverty. Two related facts change the picture: - **The 48 countries in sub-Saharan Africa (excluding South Africa) hold 14% of the world's population but produce only 0.6% of global CO2 emissions.** Even if their electricity tripled and every kWh came from natural gas, world emissions would rise by only about **0.6%** — while transforming lives. - **Indoor air pollution kills over 2 million people a year** (cooking with wood and charcoal). A short-term shift to kerosene or gas would save lives without materially harming the climate, and clean cooking gas is often paired with electrification long-term. The clean-energy path is now competitive on cost, and poor countries are structurally well placed for it. They have: - Loads of sun and wind - A large share of the minerals needed for batteries - **No stranded fossil fuel plants** to write off, so they can build modern systems from scratch The evidence that it is already happening: - **Namibia, Brazil, Chile and Morocco** already get a higher share of electricity from solar and wind than the EU or the US does - **Pakistan** has a boom in **rooftop solar** as families make their own power in response to grid instability - **South Africa** shows the same pattern after its coal grid kept failing - **Kigali (Rwanda)** banned new petrol motorbikes in 2025 to cut urban air pollution The bottleneck is not technology, it is **capital**: - Loans for a solar plant in **South Africa, India or Mexico cost about twice as much (~12%)** as in rich countries (~5%). In low-income countries the rates are higher still. - Rich countries promised **$100 billion a year in climate finance** to poorer countries by 2020. That target was **missed by about $20 billion** and only reached years late, with some money simply being old aid budgets **relabelled as green finance**. - The **G7 has blocked funding for any fossil fuel project in Africa** — while their own energy security responses to Ukraine involved firing up coal plants and building new LNG terminals.
claims.say_this: Poor countries need **energy** to develop, not fossil fuels specifically. Because those two got tangled up during the 20th century, people assume they are the same thing. They are not any more. Solar and wind are now the cheapest new power in most of the world, and poor countries have the sun, the wind, and the mineral resources to build modern grids without repeating the coal era. The catch is finance: they pay two to three times more to borrow for the same clean project than rich countries do.

pushback.if: But some fossil fuels will still be needed.
pushback.reply: Fair. Some transitional fossil use, especially gas for cooking and industry, is expected and defensible. The issue is not banning all fossil fuel use in poor countries. The issue is not pretending they are locked into fossil fuel dependence when the cheaper and cleaner path is available if the finance is there.

pushback.if: Rich countries have no right to lecture.
pushback.reply: Correct, and that is not the argument. The argument is: **the finance system, not the atmosphere, is what is holding poor countries back from clean energy**. Rich countries can either fix that (deliver the pledged climate finance, offer fair borrowing rates, stop blocking regional development banks) or stop blocking clean energy while doing nothing. The current combination is the worst option.

pushback.if: China is undercutting everyone with cheap solar and EVs.
pushback.reply: Yes — and for poorer countries that is largely good news, because it drives down deployment cost. Rich-country policy should either **help spread affordable Chinese clean tech worldwide** or build a competing industry. Just complaining about the low prices does not help anyone in the countries that most need cheap solar.

claims.claim: It says recycled on the packaging, so plastic recycling is working
heard_as: this bottle is made from recycled plastic
the brands have sorted this out
chemical recycling solved it
claims.kernel: The label is legally accurate, which is exactly what makes this one hard. Nobody is lying outright.
claims.truth: The trick is an accounting method called mass balance. A manufacturer averages a small amount of recycled feedstock across an entire production system and then labels individual products as recycled, even when the item in your hand is around 95% virgin naphtha. A 2026 Guardian and IJ4EU investigation found products from Kraft Heinz and Mondelez carrying recycled claims on this basis. The EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation legalises the approach in 2026 rather than closing it.
claims.say_this: Recycled on the label often means the company bought some recycled material somewhere in the system, not that it is in the packet. The rules allow it.

pushback.if: So should I stop recycling?
pushback.reply: No, keep recycling. Just stop treating recycled labels as proof, and push for reuse and less packaging, which is where the real gain is.

claims.claim: Renewables can't keep the lights on when the wind stops
heard_as: you need baseload power
what happens on a still winter night
we'll always need gas as backup
claims.kernel: Wind and solar genuinely are variable, and a grid that has to balance supply and demand every second cannot ignore that. Grid operators take this seriously, which is why it gets solved rather than dismissed.
claims.truth: Variability is managed with a portfolio rather than a single fix: geographic spread, interconnection between countries, storage, and shifting flexible demand to windy hours. Grid scale batteries now respond faster than gas plants can, and their costs have fallen steeply. Ireland already runs large shares of its electricity on wind for extended periods. The honest position is that the last stretch to a fully firm zero carbon grid is genuinely hard and still being worked out, while the first 70 or 80% is a solved engineering problem being deployed today.
claims.say_this: Grid operators solve this with interconnection, storage and demand shifting. The last stretch is genuinely hard. The first three quarters is being built right now.

pushback.if: So you admit you need gas backup
pushback.reply: For now, some. The argument is about how fast that shrinks, not whether renewables work. Nobody serious claims we finish this tomorrow.

claims.claim: It takes more energy to build a wind turbine than it ever produces
heard_as: solar panels never pay back their manufacturing
they only work because of subsidies
the carbon cost of building them cancels it out
claims.kernel: Manufacturing solar panels and turbines does produce carbon, and most of a turbine's lifetime emissions really do happen before it ever turns. That much is true.
claims.truth: The payback is quick. A solar panel offsets its manufacturing emissions in four to eight months and then runs for 25 to 30 years. A wind turbine takes about seven months and runs for 20 to 25 years, generating close to zero pollution once it is spinning. So a turbine spends well over 95% of its working life producing energy that is pure gain.
claims.say_this: A wind turbine pays back the carbon it took to build in about seven months, then runs for twenty odd years.

pushback.if: What about when the wind isn't blowing
pushback.reply: Different question, and a fair one. That is about storage and grid design, not about whether the turbine is worth building.

claims.claim: renewables and EVs mean a lot more mining
heard_as: Green energy needs way more mining
Renewables are just moving the mining
We'll destroy the planet with lithium mines
EVs need more resources than petrol cars
The mining for green tech is unsustainable
You're trading one extraction problem for another
claims.kernel: Because the specific pictures of lithium mines and cobalt operations in the news are real. Battery mineral demand is going up. New mines are being permitted, sometimes controversially. If you compare "a factory-made solar panel" to "a cave that already produces coal", it looks like renewables are adding mining rather than replacing it. What that framing misses is the coal that goes into a coal plant every year, and the oil and gas that constantly needs to be extracted.
claims.truth: **Mining per unit of electricity — coal is the worst by a very wide margin:** - **Coal** needs about **30× more mining than renewables** per unit of electricity - **Coal** needs about **100× more mining than nuclear** per unit - Gas needs ongoing extraction of **~125,000 tonnes of gas per TWh** of electricity **Why the numbers surprise people:** to get 1 kg of copper, miners need to dig up **160 kg of ore** and move **510 kg of rock** — copper is only 0.6% of the ore. That means the numbers already include the rock moved. Fossil fuels need the same ore-vs-usable calculation, and they do worse. **Clean energy build-out scale by 2040 (peak):** - **25-50 million tonnes of minerals per year** for solar, turbines, transmission and EVs - Sounds enormous — and it is a fraction of what fossil fuel extraction moves annually **The core insight — one-off vs. continuous:** - Building a coal plant uses fewer raw materials than building a solar plant - But the coal plant then needs a **constant supply of coal** for the whole 40-year lifespan - A solar panel or wind turbine, once built, needs no more materials. **The fuel — sunshine, wind — is free.** - So when you look at the whole picture (build + run), solar, wind and nuclear all need **far less total mining** than coal or gas **Efficiency improves the picture over time:** - Silver in a 2018 solar panel could now make **2 panels** - Silver in a 2010 panel could now make **5 panels** - Solar panels now use **⅛ the polysilicon** they needed in 2004 **Electricity vs EVs — different pictures:** - Mining for **electricity production**: falls as we move from coal to solar/wind - Mining for **EVs specifically**: might rise slightly compared to petrol cars - But when you combine both (electricity + transport), total mining still **falls significantly**
claims.say_this: Actually the opposite. Going clean means less mining overall, not more. Coal power needs about 30 times more mining than renewables and 100 times more than nuclear, per unit of electricity. And the coal has to be dug up **continuously** — solar panels and turbines only need materials once, when they're built. Yes, we do need copper, lithium and nickel for clean tech, but the total mining footprint drops sharply.

pushback.if: Look at all these new lithium mines opening.
pushback.reply: Yes — because global demand is scaling up fast. But the total volume of rock being moved for the transition is still a fraction of what fossil fuel extraction moves. And once the new mines are online, they run for decades without needing constant new coal deliveries.

pushback.if: Coal mines already exist. Renewable mines are new.
pushback.reply: That's the framing trap. Existing coal mines require constant new blasting, extraction and transport. Their impact isn't paid off, it's ongoing every day. A solar panel plant, once built, needs no more mining input.

pushback.if: Watch out for those charts saying renewables need way more materials.
pushback.reply: Some do circulate, especially the 2015-era chart that shows renewables needing more materials than fossil fuels. That chart is outdated (before solar and wind became efficient) and usually excludes the fuel burned in coal and gas plants — which is actually the biggest material cost of fossil fuels.

pushback.if: EVs really do need more mining than petrol cars.
pushback.reply: For the car alone, roughly yes. But when you add up all the mining a petrol car requires over its life (steel, aluminium, oil pumped and refined), and compare to the mining an EV requires (steel, aluminium, battery), the EV comes out closer than the framing suggests. And **when you combine transport and electricity**, the total falls sharply.

claims.claim: we need fossil fuels to build renewable energy
heard_as: You need oil to build solar panels
Wind turbines are made with fossil fuels
Renewables are just fossil fuels in disguise
It takes more energy to make a solar panel than it produces
Going green requires fossil fuels
Renewables can't reproduce themselves
claims.kernel: Because it is technically true in the narrowest sense. Cement kilns, mining trucks and container ships still mostly run on fossil fuels, so a solar panel today does have a bit of fossil fuel embedded in it. When someone points that out and says "so renewables aren't really clean," the specific fact is real. What is misleading is the conclusion drawn from it.
claims.truth: There is a specific measure for this: **EROI (Energy Return on Investment)** — how much energy a system gives back over its life for every unit of energy that went into building it. It captures exactly the concern the myth raises. - **Solar panels: less than one year** to pay back the energy used to build them. Then they run for **25 to 30 years**. Over their life they produce roughly **25 times** the energy it took to make them. - **Wind and nuclear: a few months** to pay back. They then run for decades. - **Below EROI of 1 = bad**: you lose energy overall. Nothing on the modern grid comes anywhere near this. - **EROI ≤ 5 is weak.** Once properly accounted for waste, **solar, wind and nuclear all score well above the 10 threshold** that most experts treat as "good enough" to run a modern society. The historical framing matters. **Every past energy transition used the current system to build the next one.** Timber-fired steam engines built the first coal mines. Coal-powered steel built the first oil rigs. Fossil-fuel powered manufacturing is now building the machines that replace fossil fuels. This is what transitions look like, not evidence that they cannot happen.
claims.say_this: Every energy transition works this way — you use the current system to build the next one. That doesn't mean you're stuck with it. Solar panels pay back the energy used to make them in less than a year, then keep running for 25 to 30 years. Wind and nuclear pay back in a few months. Yes, we currently need some fossil fuels to build renewables. It is a small, short-term energy debt with a very large payoff.

pushback.if: But mining and shipping are still fossil-fuel powered.
pushback.reply: Correct, and that is where the remaining work is. Mining companies are already **electrifying drills and heavy machinery**, partly because it saves them money. Panel and turbine manufacturers are moving to renewable-powered factories, again because it saves money. That is the direction of travel. The starting position for the next generation of renewables is cleaner than for this generation.

pushback.if: OK but the EROI numbers are still lower than for oil and coal at their peaks.
pushback.reply: They are for some historical fossil comparisons, but the "energy cliff" matters here. Above an EROI of about 10, extra gains barely matter for running a modern society. Solar, wind and nuclear all sit comfortably above that threshold. Chasing the highest possible EROI is not what the physics requires.

pushback.if: So we'll always need some fossil fuel input.
pushback.reply: For a shrinking share, for a shrinking time, yes. The remaining fossil use in supply chains falls every year as manufacturing itself electrifies. Nothing about physics locks it in.

Hall C., Prieto P., King C., and others
