claims.claim: renewables aren't replacing fossil fuels, they're just being added on top
heard_as: Renewables are just being added on top
There's no energy transition, it's an addition
Fossil fuel use is still going up, so nothing has changed
The world isn't really moving off fossil fuels
Renewables can't scale
We keep adding wind and solar and it never makes a difference
The transition is a myth
claims.kernel: Because if you look at global charts of energy use, both fossil fuels and renewables are still rising at the same time. It looks like renewables are just being added, not replacing anything. And in the poorest, fastest-growing economies that is broadly what is happening today: their total energy demand is rising, so both curves go up. When someone frames this as "the energy transition is a myth," the chart looks like their evidence.
claims.truth: The global picture hides three very different situations: 1. **Energy addition** — renewables added on top, fossil fuels grow as normal. **There are no clear real-world examples** of this at country level today. 2. **Energy displacement** — renewables fill demand that would otherwise have gone to fossil fuels. Fossil fuels still grow, but slower. **China** is the classic case. 3. **Energy transition** — renewables replace fossil fuels, so fossil fuel use actually falls. **Denmark, UK, Finland** are clear examples. More than **half of the world's countries have already passed "peak fossil fuels" in their electricity sector**, even while total electricity demand kept rising. - **UK**: fossil fuel electricity down by **almost half** since it peaked in 2008 - **Denmark**: down by **almost 80% since 2000** - **Finland**: down by **more than two-thirds since 2000** - Globally in **2022, renewables supplied 92% of new electricity demand**; fossil fuels the remaining 8% - Between **2010 and 2022, renewables supplied 57%** of the growth in global electricity Analysts now expect **coal, oil and gas each to hit their global peak within the next five years**. Sales of **new petrol and diesel cars already peaked in 2017**.
claims.say_this: The world isn't in one place at once. Some countries are already replacing fossil fuels with renewables and their fossil fuel use is falling — the UK, Denmark, Finland. China and most of the world are in an in-between stage: renewables are filling new demand that would otherwise have gone to fossil fuels, so fossil fuel use is growing more slowly than it would have. Almost nowhere is renewables truly "just added on top." Coal, oil and gas are each expected to peak globally within about five years.

pushback.if: But global fossil fuel use is still rising.
pushback.reply: Yes, and that is the honest bit of the claim. It hides three different stories, and one of them (real transition) is clearly winning at country level. The global total is the sum of countries at different stages — mostly at stage 2 (displacement) today, transitioning into stage 3.

pushback.if: Renewables can only replace some of it.
pushback.reply: For most of the electricity system, they can do the heavy lifting. For the last 20-30% and for hard-to-abate industry, other tools are needed (nuclear, hydro, geothermal, storage, some gas as declining backup). But that is very different from "renewables aren't replacing fossil fuels." They are, and the countries doing this are the leading indicators.

pushback.if: You're cherry-picking Denmark.
pushback.reply: Denmark is at the leading edge, but the pattern is very general in Europe. UK, Germany, Portugal, Spain, Ireland, Italy have all seen large falls in fossil fuel electricity. Outside Europe, the US has been slower but its coal fleet is now clearly in retreat. The transition looks different in different places because it started at different times and with different endowments, not because it is not happening.

sources.label: Hannah Ritchie, *Not the End of the World* (Chatto & Windus, 2024)

claims.claim: solar panels and wind turbines create huge amounts of waste
heard_as: Wind blades can't be recycled
Solar panels are toxic waste
We're just creating a new landfill problem
Nobody knows what to do with old solar panels
Renewables produce huge amounts of e-waste
The environmental cost is being hidden
claims.kernel: Because there are real photos, and they get shared a lot. A pile of old wind blades or dumped solar panels in a field is a striking image. What the photo doesn't show you is the coal ash lagoons that have been sitting outside every coal plant for a century, or the volume of oil sludge from decades of drilling. The visible dumping site is small compared to the invisible fossil fuel one.
claims.truth: **Waste per megawatt-hour of electricity:** | Source | kg per MWh | |---|---| | Coal | 89 | | Solar PV | 2 | | Wind | 0.2 | - Coal creates about **50 times more waste than solar** and **500 times more than wind**, per unit of electricity. **Waste over 25 years, for one average UK person** (if all their electricity came from one source): | Source | Total waste (kg) | |---|---| | Municipal household waste | 12,100 | | Coal | 10,700 | | Plastic | 1,900 | | Electronic waste | 600 | | Solar PV | 200 | | Wind | 20 | A person's coal waste over 25 years would fill about 10 tonnes. Their solar waste: 200 kg. Wind: 20 kg. **Toxicity matters too:** - **Wind turbine blades**: 80-85% of turbine parts are recyclable. Blades are the hard bit — hard to recycle, often go to landfill — but they're classified as **non-hazardous** in the US and Europe. Low health risk. - **Solar panels**: contain small amounts of **lead** in silicon panels, and traces of **cadmium** in cadmium telluride panels (~0.1% of panel weight). Manageable at end-of-life if collected properly. - **Coal ash**: contains **mercury, arsenic, lead, cadmium and chromium** — far more dangerous, and produced continuously for the plant's life. Switching from coal to renewables cuts both **volume** and **toxicity** of waste.
claims.say_this: Solar and wind create far less waste than coal, per unit of electricity — about 50 times less than coal for solar, 500 times less for wind. The photos of dumped turbine blades that go around social media leave out how much coal ash we've been quietly producing for decades. Renewables aren't waste-free, but they're vastly less wasteful than what they're replacing.

pushback.if: But wind blades are ending up in landfill.
pushback.reply: Some are, and this is a real problem the industry is working on. **Siemens** and others are producing recyclable blades. Several European governments are proposing landfill bans for turbine blades by the end of the decade. Compared to coal ash landfills, the volume is tiny — but "small compared to worse" isn't a reason to stop working on the specific problem.

pushback.if: Solar panels are full of toxic materials.
pushback.reply: Silicon panels contain small amounts of lead (soldering); cadmium-telluride panels contain trace cadmium. Both can be extracted and reused, and manufacturers are already doing this where end-of-life panels are properly collected. The material-toxicity issue is real but well-understood and manageable.

pushback.if: We haven't figured out recycling yet.
pushback.reply: Aluminium and glass in solar panels can already be recycled — the main materials are the same as in drinks cans and bottles. Recycling rates are still low in many countries, but most panels installed today have another 10-20 years of life. The industry has time to build the recycling chain, and countries like Germany and Japan are already ahead.

claims.claim: solar and wind take up too much land
heard_as: Solar farms are ruining the countryside
Wind turbines are visual pollution
We can't afford to give up farmland for panels
The whole planet would need to be covered in solar
Renewables destroy wildlife habitat
There isn't enough land for renewables
claims.kernel: Because it's easy to make it look scary in a photo. A picture of a field covered in solar panels, or a ridge full of turbines, activates the "they're taking over" reaction — especially in countries with strong landscape traditions. What the photo can't show you is how much power those panels produce, or how much land coal and gas actually use once mining, drilling and infrastructure are counted.
claims.truth: Land use per unit of electricity, roughly (m² per MWh, including mining and grid): | Source | m² per MWh | |---|---| | Nuclear | 0.3 | | Gas | 1 | | Solar (rooftop) | 3 | | Solar (ground, CdTe) | 13 | | Coal | 15 | | Solar (ground, silicon) | 19 | | Hydropower | 33 | - **Nuclear** is the most land-efficient way to make power. - **Rooftop solar** barely uses any new land — it sits on buildings that already exist. - **Coal** actually uses more land than most solar farms once mining and ash disposal are counted. - **Hydropower** is often the highest land-use source because reservoirs flood large areas. Wind is a special case: - **Direct land use** (the small patch where the turbine actually stands): tiny — well under 0.1% of land - **Visual footprint** (the whole area you can see turbines): 2-3% of the world if we did everything with wind - **But wind farmland is dual-use**: farmers grow crops and graze animals right up to the turbine base and get extra income from the power Powering the whole world with a single source (theoretical): - **Nuclear**: <0.01% of land - **Wind (direct)**: <0.1% of land - **Solar**: ~0.5% of land - **Wind (visual)**: 2-3%, up to 10-15% in small crowded countries Country examples: - **US** could decarbonise with **1-6% of land in solar** and **5-22% wind visual footprint** - **EU** could hit net zero with **3% of land in solar** and up to **15% wind visual footprint**. Just **1% of land as solar** would already cover EU electricity demand today. - **South Korea** and **Singapore** — genuinely too small and dense for a renewables-only path. Rare exceptions, not the norm.
claims.say_this: They need some land, but far less than most people think, and much less than fossil fuel systems when you include mining and drilling. Powering the whole world with solar would need about 0.5% of global land — much less than the half of habitable land we already use for farming. The exceptions are tiny crowded countries like Singapore. For everyone else, it's a manageable share of land.

pushback.if: But the photos of fields of solar panels look terrible.
pushback.reply: Framing matters. **The US uses 2.5% of its land to grow crops for bioethanol** — an area the size of the UK — and that only covers 10% of the country's petrol needs. Using the same land for solar would generate enough electricity to power the entire US **two to three times over**. Nobody panics about the bioethanol land use because it looks like a normal cornfield.

pushback.if: Rural people don't want turbines in their view.
pushback.reply: Legitimate concern. The fix is **fair community partnerships**: co-owned projects, discounted electricity for nearby residents, transparent siting processes. Where communities benefit, opposition drops. Where projects are imposed by distant developers with no local upside, opposition is fierce.

pushback.if: We're taking farmland for panels.
pushback.reply: Some farmland is being converted, but it's a small share of total farmland. And a lot of large-scale solar is being deliberately sited on lower-quality land, brownfields, and post-industrial sites. Rooftops and car parks can absorb a big share of demand without any farmland conversion.

claims.claim: renewable energy is too expensive
heard_as: Renewables are only cheap because of subsidies
Solar doesn't work without government handouts
Once you factor in storage, it's not cheap
Fossil fuels are still cheaper
Nobody would build solar without incentives
It only works when the sun shines
claims.kernel: Because for decades it was true. Solar panels used to be a hobbyist product. Wind turbines were subsidised. Fossil fuels were unambiguously cheaper. Anyone whose reference point is a 2000s energy debate is working from accurate memory. What changed is that between about 2010 and 2020, solar dropped ~85% and wind roughly halved, and the ratio flipped.
claims.truth: - **Solar costs fell tenfold** since 2010. In the last decade alone, ~85% drop. Analysts expect another **50% drop by 2030**. - In **2023, 96% of new solar and onshore wind projects** were cheaper than building a new coal or gas plant - **Three-quarters of new solar and wind projects were even cheaper than fossil fuel plants that were already built and running** - **Australia**: solar plus batteries about **30% cheaper** than gas peaking plants - **India**: solar plus batteries already cheaper than many existing fossil fuel plants - More than **a quarter of global emissions** are now covered by some kind of carbon tax or trading scheme Renewables get cheaper because of the **learning curve** — every doubling of installed capacity has historically taken 20-30% off the cost. Fossil fuels don't follow a learning curve. Their prices swing with world events but have no long-term downward trend. **The hidden cost of fossil fuels:** - **Air pollution**: burning coal, oil and gas causes an estimated **$6 trillion a year in damages globally** — from heart disease, cancer, stroke and lung illness (millions of premature deaths per year) - **Climate damage**: not priced into fossil fuel bills, but landing on future generations and poorer countries
claims.say_this: That was true 15 years ago. It stopped being true around 2015. Today solar and wind are cheaper than new coal or gas in almost every country, and in most cases cheaper than fossil fuel plants that are already built and running. Fossil fuels look cheap on paper because they hide huge costs — air pollution alone kills millions and costs almost $6 trillion a year globally.

pushback.if: Solar and wind are only cheap because of subsidies.
pushback.reply: That was true 15 years ago. Not any more. Subsidies helped renewables cross the initial cost gap when they were expensive. Today they're cheap because of **manufacturing scale**, not subsidies. Compare the sticker price of new solar in a competitive auction against new gas — the solar wins without subsidy in most markets.

pushback.if: When you add batteries, it's not cheap any more.
pushback.reply: Batteries add cost, and are needed to cover the intermittency problem. But solar + batteries are already **cheaper than gas at peak times** in Australia. Battery costs are following the same learning curve solar did — down about 90% over the past decade. The all-in system cost still comes out ahead in most places.

pushback.if: Fossil fuels look cheap in my energy bill.
pushback.reply: Because your bill doesn't include the air-pollution deaths, the healthcare costs, or the climate damage. Those costs are real — they're just paid by other people, mostly poorer people and future generations. That's what "hidden cost" means.

claims.claim: we're going to run out of the minerals needed for clean energy
heard_as: We're running out of lithium
There's not enough cobalt in the world
Green energy will hit resource limits
Rare earths are running out
You can't scale renewables because of minerals
Peak lithium is coming
claims.kernel: Because "we're running out of X" is a classic anxiety, and it has come and gone for oil, water, food and now minerals. Every generation gets its "peak resource" story. And the clean energy build-out really does need a lot of specific minerals in a short time. Anyone who reads a headline about "lithium shortages" is right that there is a real supply crunch. The mistake is confusing a short-term extraction bottleneck with a long-term reserves problem.
claims.truth: **Reserves are growing faster than production:** - **Global lithium production**: ~30,000-40,000 tonnes/year in 2008 → **over 150,000 tonnes/year by 2022** - **Global lithium reserves**: a few million tonnes in 2008 → **over 20 million tonnes by 2022**. Reserves have grown faster than production. **Clean energy tech would raise material demand by 5-15% overall** — not a runaway increase. Supplies will be tighter for specific materials (**lithium, cobalt, copper**), but even for these, either there's enough today or the gap is closing through new deposits, substitution and efficiency. **Efficiency gains are already happening fast:** - The **silver in a 2018 solar panel** could now make **2 panels** - The **silver in a 2010 panel** could now make **5 panels** - Solar panels use **⅛ the polysilicon** they needed in 2004 **Reserves vs. resources — two different words:** - **Reserves**: deposits that can be extracted economically with today's technology - **Resources**: known deposits, including ones that aren't economically worth extracting yet - Both categories grow as prices change and technology improves. **What the major agencies say:** - **IEA**: generally no signs of shortages in available resources - **IRENA**: no scarcity of reserves for energy transition minerals; reserves from economically viable sources have grown - **Energy Transitions Commission**: no fundamental shortage of any raw material for a global net-zero transition - **Rocky Mountain Institute**: world has enough minerals for the entire energy transition and is rapidly building the mines
claims.say_this: We're not running out. Lithium reserves have grown faster than lithium production. Every major energy agency — IEA, IRENA, Rocky Mountain Institute, Energy Transitions Commission — says there's no fundamental shortage. The real risk isn't running out; it's getting stuff out of the ground fast enough over the next 5 to 10 years, because opening a new mine takes a decade.

pushback.if: But mining takes forever to open.
pushback.reply: Yes — and that is the real bottleneck. Discovering and exploring a new deposit takes **over a decade**. Lithium sourcing takes **~4 years in Australia** and **~6 years in South America**. Once a deposit is found, permitting and construction take **~5 more years**. In the US, mine permits alone take **7 to 10 years**. That's why the next 5-10 years are the tight window — not because of geology.

pushback.if: We're already fighting over lithium.
pushback.reply: Prices are volatile because the industry is scaling up. Volatility isn't the same as scarcity. Even a big lithium price spike doesn't mean the world is running out — it means demand outpaced production for a specific stretch. New reserves are being discovered constantly.

pushback.if: What about after 2030?
pushback.reply: Substitution and recycling ease the picture over time. Tesla now uses **lithium iron phosphate (LFP)** — no cobalt — in more than half its cars. BYD is investing in **sodium-ion batteries** (no cobalt or lithium at all). Aluminium can replace copper in power lines when copper gets expensive. The 2030s look easier on materials than the 2020s.

claims.claim: This is all fine for people who can afford it
heard_as: electric cars are for rich people
green policies hit the poorest hardest
easy to be green on a big salary
claims.kernel: This is largely correct and it should be conceded immediately. New EVs, heat pumps, retrofits and organic food all cost money upfront. Climate policy designed carelessly does land hardest on people with the least, and that is how you lose public support for it.
claims.truth: Two things follow, and neither is do less. First, the people with the smallest footprints are already the poorest, and they are also hit first and hardest by heatwaves, flooding and energy price shocks, so the status quo is not neutral either. Ireland's Climate Change Advisory Council made exactly this point in 2026: fossil fuel dependence is what exposes households to price shocks, and it called for public transport investment and a fair EV transition. Second, the fix is policy design, grants, retrofit schemes, public transport, and taxing the high emitting end, rather than abandoning the goal.
claims.say_this: You are right, and that is an argument for designing this properly rather than dropping it. The people with the smallest footprints are already the ones getting hit first.

pushback.if: Politicians never design it properly
pushback.reply: Often true. Which is the thing to campaign on, because the alternative on offer is price shocks from fossil fuels we do not control.

claims.claim: wind farms kill huge numbers of birds
heard_as: Wind turbines are bird murder machines
Wind farms destroy migrating birds
Trump was right about windmills killing birds
Bats are being wiped out by turbines
Wind farms are ecological disasters
Turbines kill more birds than we're told
claims.kernel: Because it's easy to imagine, and there's a real, specific problem hiding inside it. Turbines really do kill birds. Videos of eagles hitting blades are horrifying. Certain species (raptors, migratory birds) really are at higher risk. And the RSPB — a charity dedicated to protecting birds — has publicly worried about specific wind farms. So the concern isn't invented. The question is how big it is compared to everything else killing birds.
claims.truth: **Birds killed per year in the US, by cause:** | Cause | Birds killed per year | |---|---| | Cats | 2.4 billion | | Buildings (windows) | 600 million | | Cars | 200 million | | Pesticides | 67 million | | Power lines | 28 million | | Phone/comms towers | 6.6 million | | Wind turbines | 1.2 million | Wind turbines kill **~2,000× fewer birds than cats**, and far fewer than cars, buildings or pesticides. Per-turbine figures: - Each turbine kills **4-18 birds a year** on average - **6-20 bats a year** — bats are actually more at risk than birds, as a share of population Some birds are much more affected than others: - **Birds of prey** (eagles, hawks) use hilltops to catch wind — exactly where wind farms want to be built - **Migratory birds** on flyways are at higher risk if turbines sit on their route - Killing rare or endangered birds is worse than killing common ones — a numbers-only comparison misses that.
claims.say_this: Wind turbines do kill some birds and bats. But per year in the US, cats kill 2.4 billion birds, buildings 600 million, cars 200 million, and wind turbines about 1.2 million. Wind is one of the smallest killers, not one of the biggest. And there are proven fixes — painting one blade black, or turning turbines off in very low wind — that cut deaths dramatically at almost no cost.

pushback.if: Trump was right when he said windmills kill all the birds.
pushback.reply: He said "all the birds," which is comically wrong. Turbines kill about 0.05% of what cats kill each year in the US. The RSPB, a charity dedicated to protecting birds, has built its own turbine to power its headquarters. That is not the behaviour of an organisation that thinks turbines are catastrophic for birds.

pushback.if: But it's the wrong birds — eagles and raptors.
pushback.reply: Right, and that specific risk is real. Which is why targeted mitigation matters. Fixes that reduce raptor and bat deaths without cutting energy output much: - **Turn turbines off in low wind** (bats can't fly well in higher wind, so most bat strikes happen below 5-6 m/s). Pennsylvania study: 44% bat-death reduction at 5 m/s cutoff, **93% reduction** at 6.5 m/s. Cost to energy production: tiny. - **Paint one blade black.** A Norwegian test cut bird deaths by **>70%**, and no white-tailed eagles were killed after painting. - **Play high-pitched sounds** to warn off bats. Texas trial cut deaths of two bat species by 54% and 78%. - **GPS tracking of eagles** near turbines, with automatic shutdown when they approach. - **Australian wind farm cut bird deaths 54%** while losing only **0.1%** of income. - **Cadiz, Spain**: bird deaths halved while losing **0.07%** of energy output.

pushback.if: Climate change harms birds too.
pushback.reply: Massively. Fossil fuels harm birds through climate change, air pollution, oil spills, coal mining runoff, acid rain. If you care about bird populations, the fossil fuel system is doing far more harm than the wind farms replacing it.
